Source: OA p.7 (Creating the Player Character). Rewritten in plain words. Adapted for OA Lite.

Every character in an OA game has six abilities: strength, dexterity, constitution, intelligence, wisdom and charisma. Each is scored from 3 to 18. Player characters are special: each is better than average in some way. Most need at least two scores of 15 or more just to survive an adventuring life.

A player keeps the same character over many sessions, so it matters that the player can make the character he or she wants, of a race and class the player cares about. Even an average character doesn't live long in a dangerous world, and a weak or unwanted character discourages new players. Making a character is worth doing carefully.

Rolling ability scores

The six scores are rolled. The rolls are weighted to give player characters better-than-average results. Use one of these four methods:

  • Method I: roll 4d6 and drop the lowest die; total the other three. Do this six times and assign the six totals to the abilities as you like.
  • Method II: roll 3d6 twelve times. Keep any six results and assign them as you like.
  • Method III: roll 3d6 six times and give the best of the six to strength. Do the same for dexterity, constitution, intelligence, wisdom and charisma, in that order.
  • Method IV: roll 3d6 for strength, dexterity, constitution, intelligence, wisdom and charisma, in that order. Do this 12 times, making 12 characters, and pick the one you like best.

Non-player characters

The DM should choose the scores of important NPCs, especially powerful, high-level ones. (High-level NPCs should have high scores; how else did they survive to rise so far?)

  • Ordinary NPCs: roll 3d6 for each ability. For more average results, count any 1 as a 3 and any 6 as a 4.
  • Special NPCs (henchmen included): roll 3d6 for each ability, allowing the full range of 3 to 18, except the abilities that matter to the NPC's profession. For those, use one of the four player methods, or roll 3d6 and add 1 to each die that shows 5 or less.

Wishes and ability scores

Players often use wishes (or alter reality from scrolls) to raise important or weak scores. That is a fair use of a wish and should be allowed. But raising scores has to get hard at some point, or the campaign fills with characters whose scores are absurdly high. As a guide: a wish or alter reality raises a score of 3 to 15 by one point, but a score of 16 or more by only one-tenth of a point. So one wish takes 16 to 16.1, and nine more are needed to reach 17. This limit applies only to wishes and alter reality; magic books and devices can still raise a score of 16 or more by a full point.

Source: OA p.7-9 (Character Abilities, Tables 1-7). Rewritten in plain words. The adjustment columns of OA Tables 1-7 were checked against the page images.

The adjustment numbers in OA Tables 1-7 (to hit, damage, open doors, bend bars, reaction, defense, hit points, system shock, resurrection, languages, magical attack, henchmen, loyalty and reaction) are the same as the PHB and UA ability tables the system already uses, so the character sheet works them out as usual. (OA's Table 2 gives the full weight allowance, such as 350 for strength 8-11; that is the PHB's base 350 plus its adjustment.) What OA adds is shown below, along with the minimum and maximum scores each class and race needs (see Races and Class Limits, and the Classes folder).

Strength

Strength is muscle, endurance and stamina. It matters most to bushi and samurai, who must be strong to wear armor and swing heavy weapons. Strength is the prime requisite of bushi and one of the prime requisites of samurai.

  • Samurai, kensai, barbarians and bushi with strength 18 roll percentile dice for exceptional strength (18/01 to 18/00); the note to OA Table 10 adds sohei, and the module follows the table. It improves the chance to hit, damage, the weight carried without encumbrance, and the chance to force doors.
  • Shukenja, monks, wu jen and yakuza can have strength no higher than 18 (no exceptional strength). 18/00 is the human maximum; korobokuru can reach 19.
  • As a real-world guide: strength 3 lifts at most 30 pounds overhead; strength 18 lifts 180 pounds or the character's own weight, whichever is more. No human or humanoid of normal strength can lift more than twice its own weight overhead. With exceptional strength add 1 pound per point from 01 to 50, 4 pounds per point from 51 to 90, and 8 pounds per point from 91 to 00, so strength 18/00 lifts 470 pounds.
  • To hit and damage adjustments apply to melee. A hit always does at least 1 point. For example, a wakizashi does 1d6; with strength 17 it does 2-7.
  • Weight allowance is what the character can carry without being slowed, counted in coins (10 coins weigh a pound). Up to that weight a human moves 12" a round; each extra 350 coins (35 pounds) slows him by a quarter (3" for a human).
  • Open doors is the chance on 1d6 to force a heavy or stuck door. The character can keep trying, but each try takes time and makes noise. The number in brackets is the chance to open a locked, barred or magically held door: only one try per door, and if it fails that character can never open it.
  • Bend bars/lift gates is the percentage chance to bend soft iron bars or lift a portcullis. A failed try can never succeed for that character, though he can still try to bend the bars of a gate he couldn't lift, and the reverse.

Dexterity

Dexterity covers coordination, agility, reaction speed, reflexes and balance. It is the prime requisite of ninja and affects their skills. The text says ninja with dexterity 16 or more gain +10% experience, but OA Table 12 gives ninja no experience bonus; the module follows the table.

  • Reaction/attacking adjustment applies to attacks with thrown weapons and bows (missile weapons), and to rolls for surprising others or being surprised.
  • Defensive adjustment applies to saving throws against attacks that can be dodged (fireballs, lightning bolts, boulders and so on) and to armor class. For example, Ieyasu wears a haramaki-do, sode and kote, which make him AC 6. With dexterity 16 he is AC 4; with dexterity 5 he is AC 8.

Constitution

Constitution is physique, fitness, health and toughness. It affects hit points and the chance to survive being reshaped by magic or brought back from death, so it matters to every class.

  • A character's starting constitution is the most times he can ever be raised or resurrected. Each revival lowers constitution by one. Magic can restore constitution, even above its starting score, but that never adds revivals. Once the starting constitution is used up, only a wish can bring the character back. For example, Ieyasu starts with constitution 12, so he can be revived 12 times; after that he cannot be raised or resurrected.
  • Hit point adjustment is added to each hit die; a die never gives less than 1 hit point. Only bushi, kensai, samurai and sohei can have the +3 and +4 bonuses for constitution 17 and 18. Every other class except the barbarian gets at most +2 (a wu jen, shukenja, ninja or yakuza with constitution 18 gets only +2 a die). Barbarians have their own rule (see the barbarian).
  • System shock is the chance to survive magic that reshapes or ages the body: petrification (including flesh to stone), polymorph and aging. For example, a wicked wu jen polymorphs his dim-witted hireling (constitution 13) into a tengu. The hireling has an 85% chance to survive, and must roll again when he is turned back, or die.
  • Resurrection survival is the chance to be raised or resurrected by a shukenja. If the roll fails, the character is dead for good, however many times he was revived before.

Intelligence

Intelligence is like IQ, but includes memory, reasoning and the ability to learn. It sets how many languages a character can learn (some nonhumans speak many languages, but intelligence decides how well).

Intelligence is the prime requisite of wu jen, who must be sharp to understand and memorize spells. It decides which spells a wu jen can learn and how many he can remember. The text says wu jen with intelligence 16 or more gain +10% experience; OA Table 12 says 15, and the module follows the table.

Wisdom

Wisdom combines enlightenment, judgment, guile, willpower and intuition. It is the prime requisite of shukenja; the text says shukenja with wisdom 16 or more gain +10% experience, while OA Table 12 gives the bonus at wisdom 15 and constitution 15, which the module follows. Shukenja and sohei with wisdom 13 or more get bonus spells.

The magical attack adjustment applies to saving throws against spells that attack the mind: beguiling, charming, fear, hypnosis, illusions, possession, suggestion and so on. It works automatically, without the character trying.

Charisma

Charisma is persuasiveness, personal magnetism and the ability to lead. It is not looks, though the two are linked. It matters to every character, most of all to those who deal with NPCs, hirelings, retainers and intelligent monsters.

  • Maximum number of henchmen is how many NPCs will serve the character as permanent, unpaid companions. It is an absolute limit: henchmen who die or leave because of bad treatment can't be replaced. It doesn't limit NPCs who serve for pay.
  • Loyalty base adjusts the loyalty of henchmen, soldiers and other servants.
  • Reaction adjustment applies to NPCs' reaction rolls when they meet the character. A character with low charisma starts at a disadvantage when bribing his way across a guarded bridge; one with high charisma may pay much less, or talk the guards into letting him cross for nothing.

Source: OA p.11-12 (Character Classes and Races; Tables 9 and 10). Rewritten in plain words. The tables come from the module's race data, checked against the page images. Adapted for OA Lite.

Every character belongs to a class, which works like a profession. There are ten: barbarian, bushi, kensai, monk, ninja, samurai, shukenja, sohei, wu jen and yakuza (see the Classes folder).

  • Barbarians are hunters, raiders and nomads who live by instinct and natural talent beyond civilized lands.
  • Bushi are professional soldiers from every level of society.
  • Kensai are martial artists in the purest sense, who devote their lives to mastering one weapon.
  • Monks seek a perfect union of mind and body through meditation and fighting skill.
  • Ninja practice ninjutsu, the art of invisibility: stealth, disguise, acrobatics and assassination. They can't work openly, so every ninja is also a bushi, sohei, wu jen or yakuza.
  • Samurai are elite noble warriors whose first duty is absolute loyalty to their lord.
  • Shukenja are wandering holy men: teachers, advisers and healers, respected for their devotion and magic.
  • Sohei are warrior priests, more warrior than priest, who defend monasteries and push their political claims. Their magic is limited.
  • Wu jen are sorcerers who usually live as hermits in remote places, feared and respected for their power.
  • Yakuza are thugs and extortionists, but also peacekeepers and guardians of common people. Organized bands collect payment from local merchants in return for protection.

Players who know the PHB rules should note a few differences: proficiencies cover skills beyond weapons; and most classes have special ki powers (spirit energy).

The races

Characters need not be human. There are four races: human, hengeyokai, korobokuru and spirit folk.

  • Hengeyokai are intelligent animals that can take human form.
  • Korobokuru are small, hairy folk of remote wilds, who love nature, simple art and crafts.
  • Spirit folk look human, but have nature spirits among their ancestors. They are closely tuned to nature.

Class limits by race

“U” means a character of that race can reach any level in that class; a number is the highest level he can reach; “no” means the class is closed to that race. A wish lets a character rise one level above his race's limit. Alignment limits apply to every race.

Ability limits by race

Nonhumans have minimum and maximum scores. A character whose rolled score is below a race's minimum can't be of that race. A score above a race's maximum may be lowered by the player. The limits are the same for men and women.

Two races are exceptions:

  • Korobokuru first add +1 to strength and constitution and subtract 2 from intelligence, then check the limits. If the changed scores fail the minimums, the character can't be a korobokuru and his scores go back to what they were. The changed scores can't go above 19 or below 8 (strength), 12 (constitution) or 3 (intelligence).
  • Hengeyokai must meet every limit before their animal's changes are applied. After the animal is chosen, its changes may drop a score below a minimum, but can never raise one above a maximum.

Source: OA p.12 (Korobokuru). Rewritten in plain words. Adapted for OA Lite.

Korobokuru are a small, dwarf-like people. They live in vast jungles, snowy mountain forests and barren wilds, and rarely meet humans. They like remote, harsh places of great natural beauty, where they live in simple villages or camps, moving on only when human settlement pushes them out.

They stand about four feet tall, with arms and legs a little long for their bodies, and most are bowlegged. Their limbs are hairy, the men have thin beards, and they look wild and unkempt. Most are chaotic or neutral, though they may be any alignment.

Classes

Korobokuru can be barbarians, bushi, samurai and wu jen (Table 9 also allows yakuza). Barbarians are by far the most common. Korobokuru samurai are rare; a korobokuru samurai must find a human lord to sponsor him.

Abilities

  • Ability changes: +1 to strength and constitution, −2 to intelligence, applied to the starting scores. The changed scores can't go above 19 or below 8 (strength), 12 (constitution) or 3 (intelligence).
  • Resistance: korobokuru resist magic naturally. They get +1 on saving throws for every 4½ points of constitution against magic rods, staves, wands and spells, and the same bonus against every kind of poison.
  • Senses: infravision to 120 feet; a 66% chance to recognize any normal plant or animal.
  • Combat: +1 to hit bakemono, goblins, goblin rats and hobgoblins. Giants, oni, ogres, ogre magi and titans are −4 to hit a korobokuru. (The text prints “bakernono.”)
  • Size: too small for the go-daichi (two-handed sword), any polearm but the naginata, or any bow but the horsebow. They favor spears, bows, blowguns and short swords.
  • Languages: their tribe's language, the language of spirit folk and the language of hengeyokai. They speak no alignment languages and can't learn any others. (OA also gives them its trade language, which OA Lite leaves out.)

Way of life

Korobokuru culture is much simpler than that of their human neighbors. They hunt, keep small farms in hidden places and make simple art and crafts, and they usually avoid humans. Because of this (and human conceit), humans see them as backward primitives and seldom accept them as full members of human society. Others think them rude, quarrelsome, boastful and rather comical.

Source: OA p.12-13 (Hengeyokai, Table 11). Rewritten in plain words. Table 11 comes from the module's race data, checked against the page image. Adapted for OA Lite.

Hengeyokai are intelligent animals that can change shape. There are several kinds, one for each animal, usually found on the edges of human settlement.

Changing shape is natural to them. They are not lycanthropes and have none of its signs: the moon doesn't rule them, silver weapons don't harm them more than others, their wounds don't pass the power on, and changing shape doesn't heal them.

Classes and animals

A hengeyokai can be a shukenja, kensai, bushi or wu jen. Since he isn't human, he can never be a samurai or ninja. The character must meet the race's minimum scores before the animal's changes are applied, and then chooses an animal. The traditional animals are below; the DM may add others if a player asks.

  • The alignment limits are strict and apply in all three forms.
  • Damage is for animals with natural weapons (teeth or claws), usable only in animal form.
  • Armor class applies only to the animal form, and armor or shields can't improve it.
  • Move, fly and swim are the animal form's movement; a dash means the animal can't move that way.
  • Ability changes can't raise a score above the race maximum, but can drop one below the minimum.

Changing form

A hengeyokai has three shapes: animal, human, and a bipedal form that mixes both. He can change form as many times a day as his level. So a 1st level hengeyokai who turns into an animal must stay one until the next day; a 3rd level one can change three times a day. A change takes one full round, in which the character can do nothing else. Armor and gear don't change with him, so he must arrange to store or carry them. In every form his level and ability scores stay the same, and he can speak the hengeyokai language.

Animal form

  • He looks just like a normal animal. The change is real, not an illusion, so spells that reveal illusions don't detect it. He has the movement, armor class and damage given above.
  • He has infravision to 120 feet and can speak with normal animals (who usually have only simple things to say, depending on their wits).
  • He can't use weapons, armor or equipment, and can be mistaken for (or hunted as) an ordinary animal. He can't cast spells, and can speak only the hengeyokai and animal languages, though he still understands any language he knows.
  • He has half his hit points (rounded up). Damage carries over point for point between forms. For example, a hengeyokai with 23 hit points in human form has 12 in animal form. If he loses 8, he has 15 left in human or bipedal form and 4 in animal form. He can't take animal form if that would leave him at 0 or fewer hit points.
  • A hengeyokai at 0 hit points in any form is dead. One killed in animal form doesn't change back; he is simply dead.

Bipedal form

  • He looks like an animal-headed human: he stands on his hind legs (or whatever he has) to a man's height, his front paws (or wings, or fins) become hands, and the rest keeps the animal's look, with fur, feathers, wings or tail.
  • He can speak any language he knows, human or animal, has infravision to 120 feet, can use any weapon, armor and gear of his class, and has his full hit points.
  • He loses the animal's special movement (a bipedal carp swims by the normal swimming rules; a bipedal sparrow can't fly) and moves 12". Anyone can see what he really is.

Human form

  • He looks like an ordinary human, but always keeps one telltale feature of his animal: a raccoon dog might have a silver streak in his hair, a sparrow an oddly sharp nose. The player and DM choose it.
  • He can pass as human. The form is real, not an illusion. He can use all the weapons, armor, gear and spells of his class, and has his full hit points.
  • He has no infravision, moves at the normal human rate (12"), and can't speak to animals, though he still understands them.

Language and alignment

All hengeyokai share one language, whatever their animal, and can speak it in every form. They can also talk with normal animals and speak the human trade language, depending on their form at the time.

Most hengeyokai are chaotic, though player characters can be lawful or neutral. Some animals must be good or evil, as the table shows. Humans know which animals lean which way and treat hengeyokai accordingly; a badger hengeyokai, for example, is shunned because people know badgers are evil.

Place in society

Hengeyokai are secretive, avoid long contact with humans, care little for land or rank, and never found strongholds, even if their class would allow it.

A good hengeyokai can instead become the protector of a village when he reaches the level at which others of his class could found a stronghold. He defends the land from outsiders and looks after the people, who give him food, gifts and service enough for his needs.

Source: OA p.13-14 (Spirit Folk). Rewritten in plain words. Adapted for OA Lite.

Spirit folk descend from humans and nature spirits. There are three kinds (bamboo, river and sea spirit folk), all closely tied both to the natural world and to humans. Through their human ties, all spirit folk can be samurai, kensai or bushi (Table 9 also allows monks).

They look very human, with slender eyes, small mouths, very thin eyebrows and very pale or golden skin. The men are always clean-shaven. They vary as much as humans do, but all have a hearty love of life and nature, and many come close to their society's ideal of human beauty.

Powers and duties

  • Spirit folk are tuned to nature and have special powers over natural forces and events, drawn from their spirit ancestors. All have infravision to 120 feet.
  • They also owe service to their spirit lord: the Lord of the Wood, the Lord of the Rivers or the Lord of the Sea. They must answer his summons and obey. Refusing, or shaming him, brings natural disasters on the spirit folk and their human kin. When their human kin's and the spirit lord's interests clash, spirit folk are expected to side with the spirit lord.

Bamboo spirit folk

  • They usually live near forests or jungles.
  • They have a 75% chance to recognize normal plants and a 50% chance for normal animals.
  • Alone and on foot, they leave no trail through woodland, forest or grassland. When one travels with others (spirit folk included), anyone following the group's trail is at −20% (−4 on a d20).
  • In woods or forest they hide in shadows 75% of the time.
  • Each new level, they can learn the language of one forest animal of the player's choice.
  • +1 on saving throws against spells, rods, staves, wands and miscellaneous magic items involving earth or wood.
  • Their life is bound to a bamboo grove deep in the forest. Damage to the grove does the same damage to them, and if it is destroyed they die at once. Entering the grove cures all their wounds and diseases at once. The grove can never be moved, and shoots taken from it have no special power.

River spirit folk

  • Each is linked to one river or stream and usually lives near it.
  • They breathe any fresh water and swim in any water at their normal movement (less for encumbrance). What they carry, even unprotected paper or scrolls, stays dry underwater.
  • Once a day they can lower the water of a river or stream by 10 feet for five rounds, so others can cross.
  • +1 on saving throws against spells, rods, staves, wands and miscellaneous magic items involving water; −1 on saving throws against fire attacks.
  • They speak the language of fishes.
  • Their life is bound to one river (chosen by the DM or the player) within its natural banks; water taken out of it or diverted for irrigation no longer counts. Bathing in it cures all their wounds and diseases at once. Changes to the river change them: drought lowers their hit points and ability scores for a time, great floods make them wild and uncontrollable, and damming or other engineering weakens them more and more until they die.

Sea spirit folk

  • The sea is vast, so these are the most numerous spirit folk.
  • They breathe salt water, swim in any water at their normal movement (less for encumbrance), and the gear they carry while swimming stays dry.
  • Once a day they can foretell the next 24 hours' weather, correctly 75% of the time.
  • They speak the language of the sea lords.
  • +1 on saving throws against fire attacks.
  • Changes in the sea don't affect them, and the sea doesn't heal them.
  • Once a year they can ask the sea for one favor: a violent storm, fair winds, rain, recovering a certain item from the sea floor and so on. They must ask for one specific thing. If two sea spirit folk ever ask for opposite things, neither request is granted and both lose that year's favor.

Source: OA p.28-29 (Alignment). Rewritten in plain words. Adapted for OA Lite.

Once ability scores, class and race are set, the player chooses the character's alignment: his general moral and ethical outlook. It helps the player understand where the character stands and how he responds to things. It isn't a compulsion to obey at every turn, nor a straitjacket that makes all characters alike. Characters are only human (or demi-human) and will slip now and then, but most intelligent beings follow some personal code, and alignment is a shorthand for it.

There are nine alignments, from a courteous, orderly outlook to a destructive, selfish one. Players whose characters are meant to work together should avoid the selfish end: ruthless characters seldom last where cooperation is the key to survival.

Many religions hold beliefs that match the alignments, but alignment is not religion. People of different alignments can follow the same faith. Each religion has an alignment, and tries to bring its followers to that alignment through its teachings.

The alignments are lawful good, neutral good, chaotic good, lawful neutral, true neutral, chaotic neutral, lawful evil, neutral evil and chaotic evil.

Lawful

Lawful characters believe the universe has an ordered structure. Things exist for a purpose, and only through order can that purpose be found and used. Order brings stability to society, harmony between people, and a clear chain of power and duty. Without it the world falls into chaos that helps neither community nor individual.

Law is a very common alignment. Great empires survive only through order, in which everyone knows his place and duties, flowing down from the emperor. Even in less stable kingdoms order matters: lords hold power through networks of vassals and alliances, and without order these kingdoms would break into hundreds of factions to no lord's gain. Even creatures outside these societies organize into cooperative groups, hoping order will help them reach their goals, good or ill.

Lawfulness is also inward, as in the samurai code of bushido. It sets not only the samurai's place, duties and privileges, but also how he must behave and think. To live by bushido he must discipline his conduct and thoughts and hone them for the day they are truly tested. Many major religions also stress order: ancestor worship links the present to the past, and respect for the family orders daily life.

  • Lawful good characters work to increase harmony and order in society for their own good and others'. They believe people can better themselves through organized effort. Acts against the common good must be corrected, by force if need be.
  • Lawful neutral characters want more stability in the world, without caring whether it serves good or ill. The more order and regularity, the easier life is, and order will reveal the secrets of the universe. Some major religions put order first: the harmony of understanding oneself leads to enlightenment and right spiritual growth. Good and evil exist and must be accepted, neither encouraged nor discouraged, though evil often works against the benefits of order and harmony.
  • Lawful evil characters use order and organization as tools for their own ends: tyrants who rule by force and terror, a stingy, deceitful merchant who uses the law to take others' property, a notorious moneylender. They don't care about the results of their actions as long as they profit, and will rob, destroy or cheat without remorse. Their one saving grace is that they respect laws and rules when they must. Contracts and oaths bind them unless they find a trick around them, and they rarely break their word or defy authority openly.

Neutral

Neutrality holds that everything has a balance. For every good there is an evil, for every order a disorder, and neither can exist without the other: without chaos nothing would balance order, and without evil there would be nothing for good to oppose. Many religions hold this belief, that all things are balanced (yin and yang; the book prints “ying”), and none is good, evil, lawful or chaotic without its opposite.

  • Neutral good characters think a balance must be kept between law and chaos, but don't accept that evil must be tolerated. Order and randomness can both do good. They feel no strong ties to the state or a lord, and try instead to understand how order and randomness work in society and the universe.
  • True neutral characters are very rare. It is a hard path, because the character must stay passive toward good and evil. What matters is keeping the forces in balance; a true neutral ruler stays out of neighbors' affairs unless the balance tips too far. True neutrals don't judge right and wrong, caring only whether order or chaos is gaining ground. They must be very wise to see the struggle for balance and the results of every action.
  • Neutral evil characters feel no particular loyalty, but gladly work with anyone who helps them. They often look for the easy road to fame and fortune, caring little whom they trample. They lack the every-man-for-himself attitude of chaotic characters, but judge everything by personal gain. An unscrupulous mercenary captain or a scheming tribal chief is often neutral evil, spending followers' lives for the best return. They are hard to trust, especially when paid, since their loyalty shifts with every better offer; only fear of revenge holds them back.

Chaotic

Chaos is the opposite of everything lawful. The universe has no order and never will. Everything happens by chance, and looking for meaning in it is foolish. Since there is no order, trying to impose it through society or law is pointless. A chaotic character cares only about how he feels at the moment, and believes strongly in free choice and individual will.

  • Chaotic good characters believe life has no grand plan, but that the human (or creature) spirit is noble and good at heart. Each being must follow its conscience, and by doing good can ease the suffering of others, whatever its cause. Religions of this alignment stress self-enlightenment through personal teaching, meditation and guidance: by understanding himself, a person becomes better and rises above society's limits.
  • Chaotic neutral characters are perhaps the hardest to play. To them the universe is only a set of unrelated events. They act truly at random, on the whim of the moment; good and evil don't matter. They are almost impossible to deal with, having no pattern of behavior; all that can be said is that they are unpredictable and amoral.
  • Chaotic evil characters embody the worst of the universe. They see no form or pattern in life and delight in destruction and chaos, actively disrupting order and enjoying others' pain. They act for personal gain and pleasure, trust no one, and no one sensible trusts them. They feel little pull of duty. Such beings may gather in groups, but only fear and force hold them together: the strongest bullies the rest into obeying, and any of them would gladly get rid of the leader and take his place.

Some alignments oppose each other by their beliefs. Players in the same group are strongly encouraged to choose alignments that fit together, for the sake of party harmony.

Source: OA p.30 (Languages). Rewritten in plain words. The list of languages was read from the page image. Adapted for OA Lite.

Talking matters in role playing. Sometimes actions are enough (a charging band of ragged bandits needs no words, nor does a tiger stalking through the grass), facial expressions are nearly universal, and with patience simple needs like food, help and directions can be mimed. But only when characters talk with each other and with NPCs does role playing reach its full range, so it is important to know what languages a character speaks.

How many languages

Intelligence (and for nonhumans, race as well) sets how many languages a character can learn (see the intelligence table in the PHB, which OA's Table 5 matches). That is how many he might learn in his life, not how many he knows at the start.

  1. Home language. Every character starts able to speak the language of his home country, region or tribe; it counts as one of his languages. It is far from universal; in a large empire it may be only a local dialect. Speakers of different dialects of one language understand each other about 75% of the time; among barbarians and people of the wild lands, dialects differ more and understanding drops to 50%.
  2. Second language. A character who can learn two languages also knows a widely used common tongue (unless he comes from somewhere cut off from the outside world). OA makes this its own trade language; OA Lite leaves that out, so use the campaign's common tongue (the PHB's common) instead.
  3. Alignment language. A character with a third language knows his alignment language, a specialized tongue for stating moral beliefs. It is of little use in everyday talk, being limited to the character's ethics and religious philosophy.

Nonhumans often also speak special languages: those of their race, and of creatures friendly or hostile to it.

Learning more

Once play begins, characters with enough intelligence may learn new languages: those of tribes and nations, alignment languages, ancient languages and the languages of some intelligent creatures.

Learning a language takes study with a character (player or NPC) who already speaks it. With daily lessons it takes 20 minus the student's intelligence months; for example, a student with intelligence 15 needs five months to speak reasonably well. He won't be fully fluent, but can easily make himself understood, and will always have an accent that marks him as a foreigner to native speakers.

Less regular lessons take proportionally longer: seeing the teacher every other day doubles the time. Living among native speakers halves it. Either way, only native speakers, or those taught from early childhood, ever grasp all a language's subtleties.

Multiple attacks

In OA, more classes than just fighters and their sub-classes can attack more than once a melee round:

The cycle then repeats. Attacks can be split among different targets.
  • These extra attacks apply only to melee weapons, not missiles. Weapon proficiencies (specialization) can add attacks with both melee and missile weapons.
  • Against monsters of less than 1 hit die, barbarians, bushi, kensai, ninja, samurai and sohei get one melee attack per level.

Dual-class characters

In OA no nonhuman can have more than one class, and no one can be multi-classed. A human can become dual-class, giving up one profession to learn another.

  • Requirements: scores of 15 or more in the prime requisites of the old class (for classes with no prime requisite, 15 or more in every ability with a minimum score), and 17 or 18 in the prime requisites of the new class (or in its abilities with minimum scores). Any two classes can be combined if the character meets their ability and alignment requirements.
  • The switch can happen at any level. The character keeps everything gained so far (hit points, bonuses to hit and so on), but starts the new class at 1st level. From then on all experience goes to the new class, and he can never again advance in the old one.
  • He gains every benefit of each new level except hit points, which stay as they are until he passes his level in the old class. After that he gains hit points for each new level like any single-class character.
  • Until he passes his old level he must follow all the new class's restrictions. He still has the old class's abilities and may use them at any time, but if he does, he loses all the experience he would have earned for that adventure. He always uses the better combat and saving throw tables of the two classes, without penalty.
  • Once he passes his old level, he can freely mix the two classes' abilities with no experience penalty, but must follow each class's restrictions when using its abilities. A wu jen/bushi, for example, still can't cast spells in armor. The one exception is weapons: he may use any weapon allowed to either class.

OA classes and the PHB classes

The OA barbarian is not the same as the UA barbarian; players who know that class should read this carefully.

Requirements

  • Strength and constitution 15 or more, dexterity 14 or more, and wisdom 16 or less.
  • No prime requisite and never an experience bonus.
  • Any alignment but lawful. Humans and korobokuru can be barbarians.

Hit points, combat and gear

  • Twelve-sided hit dice, one a level (see the table).
  • Instead of the normal constitution bonus, a barbarian gains 2 extra hit points a level for every point of constitution over 14.
  • Fighter combat and saving throw tables. Any armor and weapons, though the first weapon proficiencies depend on the barbarian's homeland (below).

Barbarians and magic

Barbarians hate magic and those who use it. At low levels they can't use magic items at all, and even at high levels only a few kinds. They never earn experience for finding or owning a magic item, but earn its full experience value for destroying one. At low levels they can't adventure with wu jen or spirit folk, whom they see as deadly enemies; even at high levels they distrust them. Table 15 shows what opens up with each level.

  • Climb cliffs and trees: climbs trees and natural cliffs (ledges, mountains and so on) with the chance above. Smoother surfaces such as walls are half the chance.
  • Hide in natural surroundings: hides in natural surroundings like those of his homeland with the chance above; in unfamiliar terrain, half the chance.
  • Surprise: surprises others 3 in 6, and is surprised only on a 1.
  • Back protection: when attacked from behind (a ninja included), a 5% chance per level of noticing the attacker. If he does, the attack is a normal one with no bonus for attacking from behind, and the barbarian gets a free attack on the one behind him at the end of the round. It doesn't count against his attacks that round.
  • Leaping and springing: from a standing start, up to 10 feet forward, 3 feet back or 3 feet up. With a running start, 16-21 feet forward (15 + 1d6) or 4½ to 6 feet up (4 + 1d4, each pip being six inches).
  • Detect illusion: a 5% chance per level, after one round of concentrating on his senses, never more than 75%.
  • Detect magic: 25% plus 5% per level to sense any magic except illusions, after one round of concentration, for spells and items. It doesn't detect spellcasters or creatures that cast spells, and tells only that something magical is there, not what or how it works. Never more than 90%.
  • Leadership: with barbarians of his own tribe or region, he adds his level to his charisma for maximum henchmen, loyalty base and reaction adjustment.
  • Healing: toughened by the wild, he heals at twice the normal rate. This doesn't affect cure spells or any magical healing.

Proficiencies and languages

A barbarian starts with nine proficiency slots. Up to six can be weapon proficiencies; the rest must be skills of his homeland. He speaks his tribe's language and the trade language. No barbarian starts able to read or write. Korobokuru barbarians speak only the languages their race allows.

Homelands

Barbarians come from one of three regions, and each allows different proficiencies:

  • Steppeland barbarians are roving nomads and masters of the horse. Preferred weapons: light lance, horsebow, sword and hand axe. Proficiencies: horsemanship, long-distance signaling, outdoor craft, tracking, animal handling, weaponsmith, armorer, bowyer, running, dancing, singing, weaving, tanning, sound imitation, survival and chanting. They live in leather tents, following migrating herds, and keep small herds of cattle and sheep but farm nothing.
  • Forest barbarians live in the snowy forests of small islands and coasts in the north. Preferred weapons: spear, short bow, hand axe, harpoon and sword. Proficiencies: small water craft, fishing, tracking, survival, animal handling, weaponsmithing, pottery, bowyer, sound imitation, snare building, weaving, tanning, carpentry, agriculture, singing, chanting, dancing and rhetoric. They live in small permanent villages; the women grow small crops and the men hunt and fish.
  • Jungle barbarians live in the tropical jungles of the south. Preferred weapons: blowgun, spear, sword, hand axe and dagger. Proficiencies: small water craft, fishing, swimming, survival, animal handling, carpentry, weaponsmith, armorer, sound imitation, snare building, pottery, tracking, chanting, dancing, music and sailing craft. They live in permanent villages, gathering jungle plants, hunting and fishing.

Place in society

Barbarians are outsiders to settled peoples, to whom a barbarian's birth matters little; his armed strength and wealth matter far more.

The barbarian horde

At 11th level a barbarian can summon a horde, but only in his home territory, from among his own people.

  • Size: one man for every 2,000 experience points of the leader, but no more than the area's eligible population.
  • Leaders: one aide for every 500 men (or part of 500), each of half the leader's level (rounded down), and each aide has two assistants of half the aide's level. There are also witch doctors or shamans, as suits the people. They can help with spells, but also tend to meddle and stir up trouble.
  • Gathering: the horde gathers at 500 men a week at a chosen place in the home territory.
  • Purpose: once gathered it must have a clear purpose, such as “attack the invaders of our homeland,” “pillage the settled lands” or “help the rebels against the emperor.” If the purpose changes, the horde breaks up and goes home. If it sits idle for more than a few weeks, men start drifting away.
  • How long it lasts: as many weeks as the leader's level, and even that is hard: the leader must constantly settle blood feuds and rivalries, judge claims and punishments, and guard against his underlings' plots. If the horde has taken a lot of treasure (by pillage, looting or ransom), the leader can try to hold it longer: each extra week he appeals to the horde and a reaction check is made; if it succeeds, the horde stays another week. The DM may adjust the roll for last week's loot or the hope of more. No horde ever stays together longer than 1½ times the leader's level in weeks.
  • Afterward: if the horde goes home after a successful campaign, with plenty of loot, the leader will easily raise another in the coming years and is hailed as a hero. If it failed or met disaster under him, he has very little chance of ever raising another, and can expect a cold welcome back home.

Bushi are warriors without a master: no lord, temple or monastery holds them. They are often mercenaries, bandits, highwaymen or wanderers, earning money however they can. They serve samurai, guard the court and fill out armies. A few are kensai who have fallen from that path, but most are low-born men who chose the warrior's way to get ahead.

Requirements

  • Prime requisite strength. Minimum strength 9, dexterity 8 and constitution 8.
  • Strength 14 or more gives +10% to all experience: if the DM awards 550 points, the bushi gets 55 more, 605 in all.
  • Any alignment and any race.

Hit points, combat and gear

  • Ten-sided hit dice, one a level. Fighter combat and saving throw tables. High strength and constitution give the normal fighter bonuses.
  • Any armor and any weapon.
  • Four proficiency slots at the start. A bushi may specialize in any one weapon, chosen when the character is made.
  • Bushi are often too poor to buy and keep up their armor and gear, so all start with the proficiencies weaponsmith, armorer and bowyer.
  • Going without armor teaches them to be quick on their feet: besides any dexterity adjustment, a bushi's armor class improves by one for every five levels, whether or not he wears armor.

Making a living

Bushi are often poor but seldom out of work: someone always needs a stout warrior or a strong hand. As nobles have samurai to protect them, peasants and merchants often look to bushi. The pay is poor but covers basic needs. In a friendly or neutral village or town a bushi can always find work, food and shelter, even if the food is thin rice gruel and the shelter a leaky stable.

Finding “loose” equipment. Poverty has made bushi experts at picking up gear. A bushi has a 20% chance to find any common item from the equipment lists in a village: 25% in a medium village, 30% in a large village, 40% in a small town, 60% in a large town and 90% in any city. The item is half price or free, depending on what it is. Lawful bushi always pay at least half its value (chores such as splitting wood or washing dishes can count as payment). Chaotic good bushi always pay half if they have the money. The DM decides what is available and what it costs.

Cutting purses. Bushi also cut purses or lift coins from the careless: 20% plus 2% per level. On a roll of 95 or more the attempt is noticed; any other failure simply doesn't work. Lawful good bushi may try this only when desperately poor, and only against a known enemy; chaotic good bushi only against known enemies.

Ki power

A bushi's hard life leaves little time for the reflection and mental training that help with ki, but he has a basic ki power. Charging into a fight with a fierce shout (kiai), he fights for one turn as if two levels higher: he gains the hit points, fighting ability and saving throws of that level. Wounds come off the extra hit points first; when those are gone, damage is taken normally. For example, a 6th level bushi could fight as an 8th level one, gaining 2d10 hit points and the 8th level combat and saving throw rows. The power lasts one turn and can be used once a day.

Warlord

At 9th level a bushi can become a warlord by capturing or clearing an estate and marking its borders. Then 30-60 1st level bushi come asking for places; more may come if he becomes known as a good leader who pays skilled men well. Bushi followers stay only while they are paid and his cause isn't hopeless. At 12th level, 1d6 1st level samurai ask to serve him. This is a very important event: it makes his position legitimate, close to (though not equal to) a samurai's.

Source: OA p.16-17 (Kensai; Tables 18 and 19). Rewritten in plain words. The tables come from the module's class data, checked against the page images. Adapted for OA Lite.

Kensai means “sword saint” or “sword master,” a name usually given to those who have perfected fighting with the sword. In OA it covers almost any weapon or fighting style: there are kensai of the halberd, of the sword, of unarmed fighting and so on. The player chooses the kensai's weapon. Every kensai aims to become the perfect master of his weapon; the final goal is for man and weapon to become one, acting on a single thought.

To get there, the kensai must master both his weapon and himself and study other arts. He must practice with his weapon every day, condition his body and purify his spirit through meditation and ordeal. He must learn peaceful arts and be wholly devoted to his goal.

Requirements

  • Prime requisites wisdom and dexterity. Minimum strength 12, wisdom 12 and dexterity 14.
  • Wisdom and dexterity both 14 or more give +10% to all experience.
  • Must be lawful (good, evil or neutral). Only humans, hengeyokai and spirit folk can be kensai.

Hit points, combat and gear

  • Ten-sided hit dice, one a level. Fighter combat and saving throw tables.
  • Any weapon, but no armor.
  • The chosen weapon or unarmed style comes with a free proficiency (not specialization). He starts with three proficiency slots; only one may be a second weapon, and the rest must be peaceful skills.
  • Natural armor class. A kensai gets no reaction/attacking or defensive adjustment for dexterity. Instead his natural armor class is 23 minus his dexterity (between 9 and 5); dexterity 16 gives AC 7. It then improves with level (see the table). The text says one step every three levels (3rd, 6th and so on), while Table 19 gives steps at 3rd, 6th, 8th and 10th; the module follows the table.
  • +1 on all initiative rolls, melee and missile, rising to +2 at 5th level and +3 at 9th. When fighting in a group, the bonus is his alone, so he may act before the rest of the party.
  • +1 on all saving throws. All kensai are immune to fear.

Ki powers

  • Maximum damage. Training and meditation let him focus his ki to do maximum damage with one attack of his chosen weapon. The player must say he is using it before rolling to hit; if the attack hits, it does the weapon's maximum damage plus all his other damage bonuses. He can do this as many times a day as his level (five times for a 5th level kensai).
  • Whirlwind attack (11th level). The kensai gathers all his bodily energy and becomes a blur of motion. It takes all his ki for the day, so he can't have used any ki power earlier that day, and it works only with his chosen weapon. He attacks every opponent within 10 feet once in the same round, however many attacks he normally has. Both sides roll initiative (his initiative bonuses apply) and the attacks happen when initiative says. He can't use maximum damage with it, but all his other to hit and damage bonuses apply.
  • Psychic duels. Against anyone who isn't a kensai he gets +2 on his roll; between two kensai, only their levels count.

Restrictions

  • He can never use a magic weapon of his chosen type, since it wouldn't truly test his skill, and wears no armor for the same reason.
  • Foes beaten with any other weapon earn him only half the usual experience, even if only part of the fight used the other weapon (unless he fought with his chosen weapon and another at once). Beating another kensai in a duel earns double experience. He can duel the same opponent only once per level.
  • Practice. He must practice at least two hours a day; more has no extra effect. Skipping practice does nothing at once, but before he can rise a level he must make up every missed two-hour session, practicing up to four hours a day (two for that day and two to catch up). For example, Kiyomori misses six days of practice while adventuring. When he gets home with enough experience for a new level, he must first practice four hours a day for six days.

Duels

  • Each time a kensai rises a level, there is a chance of 10 times his new level (in percent) that a kensai of that same level challenges him to a duel. A duel is a one-on-one fight in which neither side may get help from anyone. Kensai can't use magic weapons or armor in a duel. It may be a formal affair at a set place and time, or a chance meeting.
  • If he refuses, he loses his new level (dropping to the lowest experience total of his old level).
  • If he fights and loses, he loses his new level, just as if he had refused. The duel needn't be to the death; the two may agree on any terms, such as surrender, first blood or first strike, or even first draw, though that is rare.
  • From 10th level on he must win a duel to rise a level.

Source: OA p.17-19 (Monk; Tables 20 and 21). Rewritten in plain words. The tables come from the module's class data, checked against the page images. Adapted for OA Lite.

The PHB has a monk class, but OA makes them a core part of its game. Players who know the PHB monk will find this one much the same, with additions and changes to fit OA's rules.

Requirements

  • Strength, wisdom and dexterity 15 or more, and constitution 11 or more.
  • No prime requisite, so never an experience bonus.
  • No to hit or damage bonus for high strength, and no armor class adjustment for high dexterity.
  • Must be lawful (good, evil or neutral). Most monks are lawful good; very few are lawful evil.

Who monks are

Monks are ascetics trained at one of the monasteries scattered across the land. Their training builds mind and body together as a path to understanding and enlightenment. To them perfection is complete control of one's own spirit: harmony of mind and body. So they master fighting, armed and unarmed, not to become great warriors but to learn their bodies' powers and limits, while a harsh mental discipline sharpens their minds to grasp the mysteries of the cosmos. They can perform amazing feats of body and mind, but can't hold ceremonies or cast spells. They belong to a monastery but lack the religious training of a shukenja or sohei, and aren't clergy.

Hit points, combat and gear

  • 2-8 (2d4) hit points at 1st level, then 1d4 a level.
  • Thief combat and saving throw tables.
  • Weapons are limited (see Table 13 on the Classes page). No armor or shields. Using flaming oil in combat is forbidden.
  • A monk starts proficient in one unarmed martial art style and two of its special maneuvers, plus five more proficiency slots. One must go to religion and one to calligraphy; the rest are the player's choice within the class's limits.

Martial arts

What makes a monk truly dangerous is his lifelong devotion to a school of martial arts. From youth he has practiced his monastery's way of fighting. When the monk is made, the DM and player (or either) create a martial style by the rules under Martial Arts; this is his basic style. Unlike other characters, a monk gains extra attacks and extra damage with it as he rises in level (see Table 21).

  • Additional attacks are extra attacks when using his martial art. The number before the slash is the extra attacks, the number after it is how often: with a style that normally gives one attack a round, 1/4 means one extra attack every fourth round, 2/1 two extra attacks every round. Extra attacks always come at the end of the round.
  • Additional damage is extra damage with his martial art. +1, +2 or +3 is added to the style's normal damage; +1D, +2D and so on are extra dice of the style's usual type; something like +1D+1 is both.
  • With a weapon, he does 1 extra point of damage for every two levels.
  • Every monk has the special maneuver missile deflection. It isn't part of any style and doesn't use one of his style's maneuver slots.
  • Though he wears no armor, he is trained to dodge blows. His armor class is 10 at 1st level and improves with level. When fighting in his martial style he uses the style's armor class if it is better; if his own is better, he uses his own.
  • Thanks to his training he runs faster than others: base movement 15", rising with level.

  • 9th level: his ki improves: with the power he takes only half damage from any damaging magical attack even if he fails his saving throw, and none if he makes it (still once a day per level).   • 10th level: defends against telepathic and mind blast attacks as if he had intelligence 18.

  • 12th level: immune to geas and quest spells.

Restrictions

Monks see the world as passing and changeable, without anything fixed. Greed, anger and other passions block the way to perfection, so a monk must rid himself of them and all they bring. He doesn't deny that he feels them, but works to control and temper them. Besides the weapon and armor limits:

  • Possessions: a monk keeps only a tiny part of any treasure, enough for a few days' food and clothing. He may not own horses, though he may ride ones others provide, and can never hold land or property. He may keep only two magic weapons and three other magic items. All other treasure and magic items go to non-player charities and religious bodies (and leave play).
  • Magic items: leaning on magic weakens his spirit. He may use magic weapons only of types his class allows. Other magic items in OA are closed to him unless they say otherwise; DMG items only if they are rings or usable by thieves. He doesn't trade up his magic items for better ones, but keeps using the same item until it wears out.
  • Ties to the world: to cut his ties to the world, a monk drops his family name and takes a name suited to his monastery.
  • Henchmen and hirelings: none until 6th level. Then he may hire hirelings for single adventures and have up to two henchmen, perhaps one more each level after 6th. Henchmen can't be hired or bought; they must choose to join him, and can only be shukenja, bushi or ninja.
  • Conduct: he must always act morally and properly, especially toward other monks. Evil acts aren't ruled out, but oaths and the orders of his monastery's superiors bind him absolutely. He may protest gently, but argument or disobedience gets him barred from the monastery and its members' help. That matters, because to rise a level he must return to his monastery for a time of purification and enlightenment, from 10 days to several months as the DM decides. He doesn't adventure then, but lives a harsh, humble life of rituals, tests and ordeals.

High-level monks

Each monastery supports only a few monks above 7th level: three of 8th level and one of each level after that. When a monk earns enough experience for 8th level or higher, he gains that level's abilities for the time being. To keep the level, he must find and beat one of the monks of that level (or the only one). They duel in the monastery's martial style, strictly between the two; no one may step in. It needn't be to the death; usually the first one stunned admits defeat. The monk knows roughly where his opponent is. Deliberate delay, or losing, drops his experience to the minimum of the last level he held permanently: an 8th level monk who loses goes back to 98,001 points, the minimum for 7th, and must work back up.

Once he holds 8th level for good, he may live permanently at the monastery or found a branch monastery elsewhere. To found one he may save enough money to build and keep it up, but only after holding 8th level for good. The buildings and grounds belong to the order, not to him. Either way he takes on administrative duties that grow with his level.

Ninja are the invisible warriors: spies and assassins skilled in concealment, stealth, trickery, disguise, acrobatics and killing. They have special powers and many unusual devices, and their abilities and reputation are wrapped in mystery. Many people think they have supernatural powers. Ninja do nothing to stop such stories, and may spread them, since confusion makes them more feared: the mere name inspires terror.

A split class

  • Ninja isn't a class of its own. After all, ninja don't really exist; at least, that is what a ninja wants you to believe. Only humans can be ninja, and only as a special split class.
  • The character must first qualify as a bushi, sohei, wu jen or yakuza, and then needs dexterity and charisma 14 and intelligence 15.
  • Ninja have no prime requisite and never get the 10% experience bonus. A bonus earned in the other class applies only to experience given to that class.
  • Experience: a ninja splits his experience between his two classes, normally half and half, though the DM may give more to one. If he never used his ninja skills on an adventure, the DM may rightly give it all to his other class. He can advance at different speeds in the two, though they usually stay close.
  • Hit points: 1-2 hit points per ninja level, with no constitution bonus. For each level in his other class, he rolls that class's die, halves it (rounding up), then adds any constitution bonus that class allows. So a 1st level bushi/ninja has 2 to 7 hit points (1-5 for the bushi, 1-2 for the ninja). Ninja usually have fewer hit points than others of their other class.
  • Combat and saves: the combat table of his other class, but always the thief saving throw tables.
  • Weapons: besides his other class's weapons, a ninja can use the ninja preferred weapons (marked on Tables 49-51). He has two proficiency slots at the start for them.
  • Armor and magic: he can wear his other class's armor, though some ninja skills don't work in armor. He can use any magic item his other class can, plus items only ninja can use.

  • 1st level: holds his breath for as many rounds as his ninja level, once a day.

  • 12th level: passes through walls, his greatest ki power. It takes supreme concentration: he can't have used his ki for anything else that day, and must spend three rounds preparing, doing nothing else; if attacked or disturbed he loses this and all his ki powers for the day. The power lasts one round, in which he moves 1 foot per level. If he isn't all the way through at the end of the round, he dies inside the obstacle.

The ninja clan

Ninja are very powerful, so the DM must keep some control over how they are played. If the DM wishes, all the ninja in the game can come from one clan, ruled absolutely by its head. Disobeying him brings an endless series of assassination attempts, ending only when the ninja dies or kills the head of the clan and takes his place. A rogue ninja is called a nukenin, and is sometimes a hero to common people.

A ninja has two special duties: secrecy, and finishing his mission. (OA enforces them with its honor rules, which OA Lite leaves out; the DM decides how the head of the clan responds.)

  • If anyone, player character, NPC or even another ninja, discovers his true identity, he has failed in his duty. When working with other characters he must keep his identity absolutely secret; they may realize he is a ninja, but must not know who he is.
  • A failed mission can be tried again. Refusing a mission counts as defying the head of the clan, unless the DM steps in for special reasons.
  • A nukenin who survives needs twice the normal experience to rise as a ninja, though he advances normally in his other class. (In OA this follows from falling below the family's honor.)

Every ninja gets his missions from the head of the clan, though the orders may pass through others, so the DM decides what missions he takes. Because ninja can badly upset a party's harmony, the DM may decide never to send a ninja against other player characters. That is up to the DM, but strongly recommended.

A samurai is above all a warrior who lives and dies by his sword. His first duty is to serve and obey his lord (daimyo) in everything, and by doing so he gains experience and rises in power and standing. Bushido, the samurai code, is hard and unforgiving. A samurai must be ready to accept death at any moment. Serving his lord, he can't fail: he either succeeds or dies trying. If he accepts that, he cannot fail, because death isn't failure; it is the greatest service a samurai can give.

To serve his lord well, a samurai must be skilled in many things. He is expected to know the katana (sword) and daikyu (great bow) and to be a good horseman. Ideally he is also accomplished in the arts: calligraphy, music, noh, poetry and painting, almost as important as his fighting. He must strive for perfection in all of them, since they reflect on him and on his lord.

Requirements

  • No prime requisite, so no experience bonus.
  • Minimum strength, wisdom and constitution 13, and intelligence 14.
  • Must be lawful (good, evil or neutral).

Korobokuru samurai

A korobokuru who wants to be a samurai must first find a lord willing to sponsor him and accept him into his household. Until he finds a sponsor, a korobokuru samurai is treated as a bushi who can't rise above 1st level. He must choose the weapon specialization and proficiencies a samurai needs, but gets no other benefits of the class.

Hit points, combat and gear

  • Ten-sided hit dice, one a level. Fighter combat and saving throw tables.
  • Five proficiency slots at 1st level. Every samurai must specialize in the katana; the other four may go to daikyu specialization or any nonweapon proficiencies. Only samurai may specialize in two weapons at once, and those must be the katana and daikyu.
  • Required proficiencies: horsemanship by 2nd level, the bow by 3rd, and calligraphy, painting and poetry by 6th.
  • Any armor, but no shield.

He keeps the stewardship from then on, even after he rises and gains lands of his own. He may hand the duties to an underling (for a share of the tax) and need not live there. He loses it only if he fails to hand over the lord's share or badly mismanages the estate, and even then it is up to the lord to take it back; stewards have been known to seize their master's estates as their own. The land isn't his: the lord still holds it, and only the lord may dispose of it. If he refuses stewardship, his lord gives him a fitting home in the city or camp office (bakufu) where the lord keeps his headquarters.

The bushi stay loyal while they are paid, housed and fed well enough, and as long as their master's fortunes don't look too grim.
  • 9th level: he draws 2d10 1st level samurai, absolutely loyal to him as his rank deserves, and 2-7 specialists (armorers, weaponsmiths and so on) ask to serve him. There is a 10% chance one of these is a ninja sent to spy on him (as a precaution).
  • 9th level (great kiai): he gains the paralyzing shout, a burst of ki in a fierce war cry. His strength becomes 18/00 for two rounds, and every enemy within 10 feet must save vs. paralyzation or be stunned for one round. Stunned characters can't move or attack and get no armor class bonus for dexterity or shields. He can use it once a day, and not on the same day as his ordinary ki power, since it drains his inner strength so badly.

Bushido

Bushido, the way of the warrior, is a hard road. At its heart are honor, loyalty and courage. Some of its basic beliefs:

  • The samurai obeys his lord. He has the right to protest bad judgments or orders, and death is the final protest he can make.
  • The samurai is ready to die at any time. There is no failure, only death or success. Dying in his lord's service is the greatest service he can give.
  • No dishonor can go unavenged. Dishonor to lord or family is dishonor to the samurai.
  • The enemy is owed no mercy.
  • All debts, of revenge and of gratitude, are repaid.
  • Cowardice is dishonorable.

Ronin

A samurai who breaks with this code may lose his samurai status and become a ronin, a samurai without a master. (OA measures this with its honor rules, which OA Lite leaves out; the DM decides when it happens.) A ronin may have disgraced himself and been thrown out of his lord's service, or may have left on his own, especially to do something that would otherwise shame his lord (such as killing an ally of the lord who also murdered one of the character's family). From then on he is treated as a ronin in every way. He keeps his samurai abilities (except those about property and drawing fighting men) and can still rise as a samurai, but at double the experience cost.

A ronin can become a full samurai again, with his old lord or a new one, if the lord accepts him. Once he has a place, he is treated as a normal samurai again. But dishonorable acts make him distrusted, hated and, worst of all, mocked. A samurai gains little respect or power through shameful deeds.

A shukenja is a wandering priest or monk who has chosen a life of hardship and poverty. That sacrifice, with his deep faith, earns him respect from everyone, from samurai to peasant. In return he usually gives spiritual and physical help, and teaching, to those who want or need it. He has some fighting training, but his armor and weapons are limited; his main power is his spells, which enlighten, help and protect himself and others.

Requirements

  • Main ability wisdom. Minimum wisdom 12, and strength and constitution 9.
  • Wisdom and constitution both 15 or more give +10% to all experience.
  • Must be good (lawful, neutral or chaotic).

Wisdom

The shukenja's wisdom table (OA Table 27) is the same as the PHB cleric's: bonus spells of one 1st level spell at wisdom 13 and another at 14, one 2nd level spell at 15 and another at 16, one 3rd level spell at 17 and one 4th level spell at 18; a chance of spell failure of 20% at wisdom 9, 15% at 10, 10% at 11, 5% at 12 and none from 13. A shukenja needs wisdom 17 to cast 6th level spells and 18 for 7th level spells.

  • Shukenja and sohei with high wisdom get the bonus spells, but only at spell levels they can already cast. The bonuses add up: a shukenja with wisdom 15 has two extra 1st level spells and one extra 2nd level spell, though he can't cast the 2nd level one until he reaches 4th level.
  • Chance of spell failure is the chance that a spell has no effect at all. Roll every time a spell is cast; on that number or less the spell is used up and fails completely.

Religion

A shukenja serves a religion, but the player needn't pick one. All religions are respected and honored, and common people mix the practices and beliefs of one with another. Faith and ritual are woven into daily life. Temples are everywhere, each more or less independent, whatever god or gods it serves.

Hit points, combat and gear

  • Six-sided hit dice, one a level. Cleric combat and saving throw tables.
  • Armor no heavier than studded leather, though some single pieces of armor are allowed, and limited weapons (see Table 13 on the Classes page).
  • Six proficiency slots at 1st level, only two of them weapons. Of the other four, one must be religion and one calligraphy; the last two can be any nonweapon proficiency.

Training

Before he sets out, a shukenja trains at a monastery or temple in three things: ritual, meditation and self-defense.

  • Ritual: he can perform marriages, christenings, funerals, holy day observances and purifications. A purification can lift curses and ward off evil. He has a 5% chance per level to remove any curse with a purification. To ward off evil, he sanctifies an area of 5 feet radius (75 square feet). At the end of the ritual, everyone in it gets +1 to hit and on saving throws when fighting evil spirits, as long as the shukenja stays inside the purified circle. Several purifications don't add together.
  • Meditation: deep concentration that restores his energy. An hour of unbroken meditation is as restful as two hours' sleep. While meditating he ignores hunger, thirst, heat and cold, but stays conscious and aware, so he suffers no penalty to surprise or initiative.
  • Self-defense: a free proficiency in one unarmed fighting style of the player's choice, not using one of his starting slots.

Ki power

A shukenja can focus his ki to resist an attack in body and mind, gaining +3 on a saving throw. He can do this as many times a day as his level, and may decide at any point in a round, but not after the saving throw is rolled; once the die is rolled, the result stands.

Experience

  • Shukenja aren't warriors, so they earn only half experience for killing or defeating humans and monsters, but full experience for defeating evil spirits.
  • Sworn to poverty, they earn experience for treasure only when it is given to charity or the poor.
  • Unlike others, they earn experience for using healing and curing spells on others: 100 points per spell level used to heal, cure or similarly aid an NPC or creature not connected with the party.

Rules of conduct

A shukenja's religion forbids him to eat meat, requires him to avoid violence (especially killing) whenever he can, and forbids excess in drinking and eating. Breaking these rules brings a punishment chosen by the DM, typically loss of spell levels or a special penance. Sometimes a shukenja is forced to break them; the DM should take that into account when choosing a punishment. A particular religion may add other rules, at the DM's discretion.

Learning spells

A wu jen's intelligence table (OA Table 32) is the same as the PHB magic-user's: chance to know each listed spell 35% at intelligence 9, 45% at 10-12, 55% at 13-14, 65% at 15-16, 75% at 17, 85% at 18 and 95% at 19 or more; minimum spells per level 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10; maximum 6, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18 and all. Check only the spells of levels he can learn, and each new level as he becomes able to cast it.

  • Chance to know: the chance he can learn a given spell. When the character is made, check each spell once, in any order the player likes, so he can check the spells he wants most first. On the chance or less he understands the spell and can learn and cast it. He still has to find a written copy, learn it from someone who knows it, or research it. Each time he becomes able to cast a new level of spells, check each spell of that level.
  • Minimum spells per level: if after one full pass through the list he understands fewer than this many, he goes through again, checking the ones he missed, until he reaches the minimum.
  • Maximum spells per level: once he understands this many spells of a level, he can't check any more of that level.
  • Understanding, knowing and remembering a spell are three different things. Understanding means he can grasp how it works when it is first described to him, spoken or written. Once someone explains it and he understands it, he knows it and can write it in his spell book. Even then he can't cast it until he studies it in his book and memorizes its details.
  • Example: Hideyori, a 1st level wu jen with intelligence 16, has a 65% chance to understand any spell, and can know at least seven and at most 11 of each level. The player picks the spell he wants most, cloud ladder, and rolls 32, so Hideyori understands it, though he can't cast it until someone teaches it to him. The player goes on until Hideyori understands 11 spells or every spell has been checked once. After one pass Hideyori understands 10, which is over his minimum, so he can't check any spell twice. But since he may understand 11 1st level spells, if he comes across another (on a lost scroll or in a borrowed spell book) he can check it.
  • If his intelligence drops for more than a short while, roll for each spell he understands, in any order; a roll over his chance means he no longer understands it. Keep going until he has forgotten enough to fit his new maximum. If his intelligence rises and his maximum goes up, he can try to understand new spells as he finds them.
  • New spells can be learned from a teacher, another wu jen's books (though few wu jen will lend such a treasure) or a magic scroll, which is destroyed in the process.

Ki powers

To learn his spells a wu jen follows a strict mental discipline. He learns to meditate as a shukenja and develops two ki powers, each usable once a day:

  • Sudden action: focusing his ki, he bursts into action, with +3 on initiative for one round, which makes him dangerous in a critical fight.
  • Maximum effect (4th level): he summons great magical energy to cast one spell at least three levels below his own level at maximum effect: maximum range (if he wants it), duration and effect. A 4th level wu jen can cast a 1st level spell this way.

Mastering an element

Wu jen spells fall into five elements: earth/metal, water, fire, wind and wood/nature. A wu jen who has learned every spell of one element up to the highest level he can cast is a master of that element. His spells of that element then give a −1 penalty to saving throws against them and do +1 damage, and he gets +1 on his own saving throws against spells of that element. When he becomes able to cast a higher level, he is no longer a master until he learns all of that element's spells at the new level.

Pupils and strongholds

At 10th level a wu jen draws 1d4 pupils, all 1st level wu jen, who serve him faithfully until they reach half his level and then leave. Each one who leaves is replaced by another 1st level wu jen who wants to study with the master. A wu jen draws no bodies of fighting men, but he can hire them and build a stronghold; not being a warrior, he must also hire a lieutenant to command them.

Languages

Wu jen speak the languages of tengu and oni. Their dealings with these creatures give them +20% on reaction rolls when they meet them.

Taboos

Because their power comes from supernatural sources, wu jen live under taboos that don't affect anyone else. They may seem silly or unimportant to others, but they are vital to a wu jen: breaking one brings loss of spells, illness or other misfortune. A wu jen has one taboo at 1st level and takes another for every five levels he gains. The player chooses, and if he suggests a fitting new taboo, the DM should allow it. The DM may also invent others, as long as they are as restrictive. Some examples:

  • Can't eat meat.
  • Can't have more treasure than he can carry.
  • Must make a daily offering (of food, flowers, incense and so on) to one or more spirit powers.
  • Can't bathe.
  • Can't cut his hair.
  • Can't touch a dead body.
  • Can't drink alcohol.
  • Can't wear cloth of a certain color.
  • Can't light a fire.
  • Can't sit facing east (or north, south and so on).

What a yakuza is depends on whom you ask. He has been called a protector of the common man, a thug, an extortionist, a rowdy, a thief, a mercenary, a jack-of-all-trades and even an unofficial police force. He is despised and respected at once, and sometimes even backed by the local lord. On one hand he stands for the shadowy underworld and runs its illegal trades; on the other he protects the helpless and watches over those in his care. That fatherly care has a price, and it is his living. A yakuza's powers come from dealing with people, so the class works well only in towns and cities; in the countryside his life is lonely and hard.
