Contacts

Contacts are NPCs who give the yakuza special information and help. They won't adventure with him, but will buy stolen goods, hide him, carry messages and pass on information. They never do anything that puts them in danger, though they may risk their reputations. They stay helpful, and quiet about his doings and their part in them, as long as they are treated fairly, not threatened and not implicated in anything.

  • A yakuza has one contact for every two levels.
  • Contacts aren't set in advance by the DM or a table. When the player wants to use one, he names the contact and his position and tells the DM, who decides whether it fits. The contact can be no more than four levels above the yakuza, and the yakuza must have had some believable reason to meet him in the past.
  • If the DM accepts the contact, his details go on the character sheet and one of the yakuza's available contacts is used up. After that he can use the contact again whenever he needs. (The DM may note details and give the contact a fitting personality.) The player keeps track of his contacts' names.
  • Examples of suitable contacts: a ward's gatekeeper, a ship's captain, a minor samurai in a lord's service, a district magistrate, a rich merchant. In the end it is the DM's judgment.

Ki power and dealing with people

  • Ki: by focusing his energy, he senses and anticipates an opponent's moves for a moment, and shifts to lessen the danger of an attack (sidestepping at the last instant, partly blocking the target and so on). It doesn't stop the attack, but halves the damage he takes (rounding up). Usable once a round, as many times a day as his level.
  • Dealing with people: a successful yakuza soon masters knowing when to threaten, coax, befriend, bribe or persuade. He gets +10% on encounter reaction rolls, except where social standing is involved.

The yakuza band

On becoming a yakuza he is adopted into a yakuza band (kumi), organized like a family: a head (oyabun), uncles, fathers and brothers. He is expected to treat them as blood relatives, and some may be.

  • Stipend: each month he receives 10 gp per level from the band (OA: 2 ch'ien).
  • Brethren (2nd level): he can call on some of his brethren (kyodai-bun) to help in an undertaking, once per level. He may call up to his level in brethren, but needn't call them all. They must be at least one level below him and never above 8th level. Once called, no more can be called until his next level. Major undertakings must be approved by the oyabun.
  • Territory: every yakuza band has a base of operations, its territory, which it guards jealously as the source of its income and power. Bands wage secret wars and feuds to keep or seize a district of a city. Since these territories aren't official lands, they can exist inside other states. The center is wherever the oyabun keeps his headquarters. A new yakuza is given a small part of the territory, and is responsible for more as he rises.
  • Tattoos: yakuza show membership and rank with tattoos. He starts with a small tattoo on his arm, and each new level adds another part of his body. The face, hands and feet are never tattooed, but high-level yakuza have their whole back, chest and arms covered. Everyone knows what the tattoos mean and soon learns not to bother such a person.

The yakuza and the law

Though the government sometimes tolerates, allows or even recognizes them, yakuza are still criminals. They can always be arrested and punished for their crimes, from prison to humiliating execution, and must always beware the law. Because of this it pays the band to keep everything in its territory running smoothly and quietly. It strictly controls every undertaking there; superiors oversee all its activities and report to the oyabun. When a yakuza or a stranger makes trouble in the territory, the band acts quickly and efficiently: the troublemaker may be hunted down and killed, handed to the police or driven off. In this way the band works as an unofficial arm of the police, preventing trouble and lightening the official police's work.

Many of these weapons are unusual in name or use. Each one's description, with any special rules, is on its compendium entry. These have rules of their own worth knowing before play:

  • Counts as a small shield: gunsen, and the sang kauw in its buckler form.
  • Hidden or tool weapons: kiseru (pipe), kumade (climbing rake), nekode (climbing claws, +5% to climb), ninja-to (with its many-purpose scabbard), shakujo yari and shikomi-zue (spears disguised as staffs).
  • Ninja tricks: metsubishi (blinding powder), needles (spat from the mouth), tetsu-bishi (caltrops).

The katana and the daisho

For a samurai, the katana is more than a sword: it is part of who he is. It is his personal weapon, not for others to use. Touching the scabbard of his sheathed katana insults him, and so does drawing the blade without his permission. A katana may have been in a family for generations, and losing it is a disgrace that only recovering the sword and punishing the takers can wipe away; many samurai have died trying. The price on the list is for an average blade; others cost more or less with their quality, workmanship and history.

A wakizashi that is part of a matched set is treated the same way. The katana and wakizashi worn together are the daisho ("long and short"), and in many lands they mark a samurai's rank: only samurai may wear both. Anyone else who does can be arrested or executed on the spot for claiming a rank he has no right to.

The armor here suits warm lands: steaming jungles, humid forests and blistering steppes. A man sealed in metal could cook inside it, or watch his armor rust until the joints lock, the hinge pins shear and the plates rot away. It also suits a way of fighting that prizes speed: the steppe rider who strikes suddenly, the ninja slipping unseen through a camp, the samurai who falls from his horse and lands on his feet, the monk who strikes fast and dodges every blow. A warrior's speed counts for more than heavy protection.

So armor here is made to resist the weather, move freely, stay light, and look colorful and artistic. Heavy metal armor such as field plate is seldom seen. Armorers work instead in leather, brigandine, mail and lamellar (laced) construction.

  • The most common armor is cloth and leather. Foot soldiers wear quilted cotton or padded leather. Higher-ranking warriors may have hardened leather scale or brigandine.
  • Chain mail is often worn hidden under clothing, or sewn in among rich silks and soft dyed leathers.
  • Now and then a noble has armor of metal bands. Solid iron and steel are kept for helmets and vital areas.
  • Laced armor is made of small metal plates tied together with colored leather lacing, then carefully lacquered against damp. It is colorful, elaborate and painfully slow to make. The lacings form rows of bright patterns; sections may be covered with painted leather, edges trimmed in red copper, and each part tied down with red silk cords to sculpted bosses of copper, silver or gold. Each piece is a work of art, and complete sets are rare, being so costly and slow to make.

Suits and pieces

In OA, all armor is either a suit or a piece.

  • A suit is a complete set that protects the whole body. The most common are padded, leather, studded leather, leather scale, chain mail and brigandine. Metal scale, splint mail, banded mail and laced suits are rare. Plate mail, field plate and full plate are virtually unknown.
  • Pieces are made of laced armor in many shapes and colors, and each protects part of the body.

Grenades

Ninja often carry grenades. They don't explode with force: they are blown-out eggshells (or hollowed nutshells, or paper packets) filled with powders, used to blind foes and cause distractions.

  • Throwing one takes a normal to-hit roll, using the rules for grenade-like missiles to find where a miss lands. Armor doesn't change the roll, since the powder bursts into a small cloud on impact.
  • Pepper: affects one target, who must save versus poison or be helpless for 1-6 rounds from choking and sneezing.
  • Dust: the same, except the victim is blinded for 1-6 rounds.
  • Flash powder: must be thrown onto a fire, where it flares brilliantly. Everyone looking at the light is blinded for 1-3 rounds. Anyone who may or may not have been looking saves versus petrification to avoid it.
  • Poison smoke: must also be thrown onto a fire. It bursts into vile, stinking smoke that spreads 5 feet by 5 feet a round, up to a 10 foot by 10 foot area per grenade. Everyone in it must save versus poison or be blinded and helpless from the acid stench, and everyone in it takes 1-2 hit points of damage a round. The smoke lasts one turn or until the wind blows it away.
  • Eggshell grenades are fragile and must be packed carefully. If a character carrying them falls 10 feet or more and takes damage, each grenade must save versus crushing blow.

The rate of fire and ranges for grenades are on the Weapons page (Table 51).

Barding

Like shields, barding varies from land to land, and even where it is used it is rarely as heavy or complete as the barding in the PHB; bad weather and the need for speed limit armor. It is usually seen only on the mounts of important nobles, generals and shock troops.

  • Sizes: half barding covers the horse's head, neck and forequarters; full barding covers the whole body. Half barding is more common.
  • Materials: most often quilted and padded cotton, then (in rough order) leather, leather scale, brigandine, metal scale and chain mail. Plate barding is never used.

Weapon proficiencies

  • A character can take a proficiency in any weapon his class allows. It costs one slot, and it is noted on his character sheet.
  • Unarmed combat can't be taken as a weapon proficiency unless the character is studying under a master.
  • A character can pick up and use a weapon his class doesn't allow, but always with his class's non-proficiency penalty (the worst one, for a split class character), and he can't keep and carry it to use later.
  • Some characters can't use some weapons at all, whatever the penalty: a character under 5 feet tall can't use a weapon over 12 feet long; one under 4 feet tall can't use the daikyu (great bow); one weighing less than 100 pounds can't use a heavy crossbow, a two-handed sword, or any weapon weighing more than 200 gp.

Weapon specialization

Only samurai and bushi can specialize. A specialist trains and disciplines himself in one weapon. His dedication isn't as fierce as a kensai's, so he doesn't gain a kensai's abilities, but he can learn other weapons more easily than a kensai.

  • Cost: specializing in a melee weapon or a crossbow costs two slots; in any other missile weapon, three.
  • Bushi: can specialize in any one weapon, chosen when the character is created.
  • Samurai: can specialize only in the katana and the bow, and is the only character who can specialize in two weapons at once. He must specialize in the katana when he is created; he can put off the bow until later.
  • The weapon must be one specific weapon, not a group: a character can specialize in the katana, but not in all swords.

Melee weapons:

  • +1 to hit and +2 damage with the weapon.
  • The character knows iaijutsu (fast draw) with the weapon and gets its benefits (see the iaijutsu proficiency).
  • He uses the next higher row of the Multiple Attacks table with this weapon. A 1st level samurai makes 3/2 attacks a round with his specialized weapon; at 5th level he makes 2.
  • After 1st level, one more slot gives double specialization: +3 to hit and damage.

Bow:

  • The specialist gains a "point blank" range of 5 to 30 feet, besides short, medium and long. At point blank range he is +2 to hit and damage and his base damage is doubled; strength and magic bonuses to damage aren't doubled but are added after.
  • At short range he is +1 to hit. At medium range and beyond he has no special bonus to hit, and beyond point blank range no damage bonus.
  • If he starts the round with an arrow ready (nocked, drawn and aimed at a target), he fires before initiative is rolled.
  • At higher levels he gains more shots, as shown on Table 57.

Crossbow:

  • Point blank range is 5 to 60 feet, with the same benefits as for the bow.
  • +1 to hit and damage at short range; +1 to hit at medium range.
  • The same benefit for having the weapon ready at the start of the round.
  • Extra attacks a round, depending on the kind of crossbow, as shown on Table 57.

Characters are expected to be more than warriors, priests or magicians: to be complete, they must also be skilled in the arts. Among the well-born, contests in poetry, painting and other arts are frequent and popular. Winners gain experience; losers risk humiliation and lost favor. Players do well to make their characters skilled in many things beyond their profession.

The four lists

  • Peaceful proficiencies are grouped as common, artisan, court and barbarian.
  • Only barbarians can learn barbarian proficiencies.
  • The other lists show where a character must be to learn a proficiency, and help the DM choose proficiencies for non-player characters: a peasant knows proficiencies from the common list, a noble from the court list.

Learning

Peaceful proficiencies have no set study time. An adventure doesn't fill every minute of a character's life; there are gaps between adventures and idle hours during them, and he is assumed to spend that time practicing a weapon or polishing a skill.

To learn a proficiency, he needs the tools at hand and, when he first learns it, a place where people skilled in it can train and guide him. To learn poetry, he must have spent time at a court or noble house where poetry is practiced, comparing his work with the masters' and learning proper forms, imagery and subjects. To learn weaponsmithing, he must live among skilled smiths. How much contact with the masters he needs is left to the DM.

The base number

  • Weapon proficiencies improve on their own as the character rises in level; that is built into the combat tables. Peaceful proficiencies don't.
  • Each peaceful proficiency has a base number. Like a to-hit roll, the character must roll that number or more on 1d20 to succeed.
  • The number never improves just because the character rises in level. From 2nd level on, he can spend more slots on the proficiency; each extra slot adds +1 to his roll. There is no limit to the slots he can spend, but after all modifiers he never succeeds on less than 3.
  • Magic items that improve a proficiency help only a character who already knows it; the item's description says how.

Example: the samurai Torimatsu Akimori learns calligraphy, a court proficiency open to samurai, spending the two slots it needs at 1st level. Its base number is 17 in this example (Table 61 prints 18; the compendium uses the table's 18). At 3rd level he spends another slot, and is +1 on the roll, so he succeeds on 16. At 4th level, getting ready for a major contest at court, he spends two more slots: he is now +3 and succeeds on 14.

Success and failure

  • For most peaceful proficiencies there is no clear success or failure. A character who knows a proficiency can use it properly whatever the roll. A farmer doesn't roll to remember how to farm, and a carpenter doesn't fail to build a house because of a bad roll. Usually no roll is needed at all.
  • When the quality of the work matters, roll. Equal to or above the base number means superior work; below means average work, or worse on an exceptionally bad roll. The farmer has a fine, average or poor harvest; the carpenter builds a handsome, well-designed house or one that is drafty and leaks.
  • Some proficiencies, such as weaponsmith and armorer, have a clear success or failure: a botched effort can leave the item useless. These are always rolled, and are marked "Always rolled" in the tables below.

Contests

Contests in the peaceful arts are a regular part of life among the well-born. Winners gain experience, and the results can greatly change a character's standing.

  • Formal contests are most often held at court or in noble households and announced ahead of time. Often a subject is set and contestants bring a finished work; sometimes there is none, and the contest tests improvisation. No one has to attend, but those who want their lord's favor or a political post seldom miss a chance to appear at court.
  • Informal contests can happen whenever nobles gather. A host watching a beautiful moonrise with his guests may suddenly ask them for a poem about it. Experience for winning is less than at a formal contest. Characters should be ready for anything.
  • Who wins: each contestant rolls 1d20 against his number. A failed roll puts him out (he has lost). Keep rolling until one contestant is left; he wins. If everyone fails the first roll, the contest is inauspicious (held on an unlucky day, perhaps): there is no winner.
  • Experience for winning: 50 times the host's level for an informal contest, 100 times for a formal one.

Optional bonuses

If the DM likes, he can give a one-time bonus for what the player does, not the character. A player who offers an example of the art that fits the moment (a piece of Chinese or Japanese poetry, say) can get +1; one who actually performs it (writes a haiku, for instance) can get +2. This rule is optional, and DMs and players who use it must find their own sources on the forms of these arts.

The proficiency lists

"Slots to learn" is the number of slots it takes to learn the proficiency. After that, each improvement costs one slot, however many it took to learn. Descriptions, with special rules (armorer, bowyer, weaponsmith, tracking, horsemanship, iaijutsu and others), are on each proficiency in the OA Lite Proficiencies compendium.

Spells matter most to shukenja and wu jen, and to a lesser degree to sohei, and they shape play a great deal. Each spell is a particular power, set off by its components:

  • Verbal (V): words the caster speaks. A caster who can't speak can't use these spells.
  • Somatic (S): gestures, mostly of the hands. The caster's hands and arms must be free for the whole casting.
  • Material (M): things that are written on, burned, shaken, tossed in the air and so on. Most are common, but some spells need elaborate preparation. Without the material components, the spell can't be cast at all.

How many spells a character can use depends on his class and level (see his class page). High ability scores and magic items may raise the number.

Shukenja

Spells are the holy man's armor and sword, signs from his deity of the power of his faith and his religion. He shouldn't hold back from using them out of fear of pride.

  • Helper: each spell is a living lesson in the shukenja's calling, and many of them aid, comfort and guide others. Through these services he teaches the noblest values. He should never refuse his services to the needy or unfortunate, nor use them for personal gain, but for the good of his religion. His goal is to give aid and comfort to the weak and helpless, as a living example of his faith, and his experience awards reflect this.
  • Adviser: he also advises and guides others, and many of his spells help find the best course of action, some for the crisis at hand, others giving insight into what the future probably holds. In a party, he is the wise man whose words should be heeded: guide, teacher and sage. His advice isn't always perfect, but others would do well to listen.
  • Protection: the world isn't perfect, so some of his spells protect him, mostly defensively. He doesn't want to crush his foes, but sometimes must, so he has a few offensive spells. They are rarely severely harmful; he has no wish to cause death and anguish.
  • Reversed spells: some spells can be cast for the opposite effect, as the description says. Using some reversed spells can call the shukenja's faith into question. Careless misuse brings his deity's disfavor (loss of levels or experience), and flagrant disregard leads to a change of alignment. The DM decides the final consequences.
  • Getting spells: he meditates for at least six hours, cleansing his mind and preparing himself as a vessel for his deity's purpose, and then chooses his spells. Choosing is part of his training: how can he help others without the foresight to see his own needs? A cast spell is forgotten until he composes his mind again, because the spiritual power passing through him disturbs the harmony of his mind.
  • Sohei use shukenja spells, but only those marked for sohei (see Shukenja Spells).

Wu jen

Spells are the wu jen's main tool: to defend, attack, investigate and research. His spells are often more dangerous and powerful in combat, single or mass, than a shukenja's, but he can do little for the injured, sick and unfortunate beyond a few spells and his own skills. His magic has neither the limits of mercy and kindness nor their benefits.

Common folk often fear him: a man of unknown mysteries who gave up comfort and company to learn secret lore. That lore is taught only by those who already have it, and masters choose pupils carefully for dedication, cleverness and talent, then reveal their secrets slowly and jealously, fearing rivals and misuse.

Students are taken young and spend years in solitude. At first a student is little more than a servant: he rises early, fetches water, cooks his master's meal, spends hours fetching odd items and cleaning, eats his bowl of rice at midday, then meditates for hours (a twitch earns a sharp blow of the master's cane). Then he studies forgotten languages and the secret meanings in everyday words, practices calligraphy with brush and ink (vital to magical work), cooks his master's dinner, studies the ancient classics, and sleeps a few hours well after dark before starting again. As he proves himself, the master teaches him more of the secrets of casting.

  • No spell book: unlike a magic-user, the wu jen keeps no spell book. He has a collection of scrolls and books, classic treatises of lore; each scroll is a commentary on the art and discipline of casting one spell, full of philosophy and metaphysics.
  • Memorizing: the scrolls are complex and exacting and must be studied before any spell is memorized. He needs at least six hours of restful meditation and study with his scrolls. A cast spell is forgotten until memorized again, because the release of mystic energy upsets his delicate mental balance.
  • Starting spells: a new wu jen has just left his master, carrying a few nonmagical scrolls he copied from his master's collection, recording the 1st level spells he knows. Roll 3d6 for how many. If the roll is below the minimum for his intelligence, he has the minimum; if above the maximum, he has the maximum. The player chooses the spells from the list. No percentile roll is needed for these, since his years of apprenticeship trained him in them.
  • New spells: each time he finds a treatise on a spell he doesn't know, roll percentile to see whether he can master it. He can never have fewer than his minimum or more than his maximum spells per level.
  • Reaching a new spell level: the DM picks one of two ways. If master and student are still friendly, the wu jen can return and spend a month studying and copying his master's scrolls, gaining spells as he did at 1st level; the DM can rule that the master lacks some spells (this works best if the DM makes the master a non-player character with a set level and spell list). Or the wu jen must find new spells himself, in other wu jen's scrolls or forgotten on dusty shelves in temples and academies, so he may gain few or none of the new level when he advances. Either way, the DM secretly determines which spells he can learn (based on intelligence), within the minimum and maximum. Players should ask their DM which way is used.

Reading a spell description

Spells are listed by level, alphabetically within each level, in the OA Lite Spells compendium. Each gives its type, level, range, duration, area of effect, components (V, S, M), casting time and saving throw, then a description. Spells that also appear in the PHB or UA are included in short form, so no one has to look through other books.

  • Range is in inches (meaning tens of feet or yards) or "touch". A touch spell means the caster must touch the target. Against an unwilling target he needs an unmodified to-hit roll; if it misses, the spell still goes off but is wasted.
  • Duration is how many turns or rounds the spell lasts. "Permanent" lasts until something removes it, if anything can. "Instantaneous" is a brief flash, almost impossible to avoid.
  • Area of effect is how big an area, or how many creatures, the spell affects.
  • Casting time is in rounds or segments: 10 segments to the round, 10 rounds to the turn.
  • Saving throw says whether a save is allowed, and whether it halves the effect (1/2) or cancels it (neg.).

The properties

  • Armor of quality: not magical, but so finely made that it is light and very flexible. No armor class bonus, but it counts as one encumbrance class lighter than normal. It is decorated with fine taste, worth 2d4 times the normal price. A character with the armorer proficiency can make it (see the proficiency).
  • Etherealness: makes the wearer ethereal, as armor of etherealness in the DMG.
  • Vulnerability: works as armor of vulnerability in the DMG. Its +1, +2, +3 and so on (from Table 76) is really a penalty to the wearer's armor class.
  • Missile attraction: cursed; works like the DMG's missile attractor shield for deciding whether the wearer is the target of a missile attack. Its plus is really a penalty to armor class.
  • Presence: gives the wearer a dignified, commanding air. For all encounter reactions he counts as having charisma 18. Friendly troops within 12" get +10% morale. The armor is very distinctive and works only when seen, so the wearer can't hope to blend into a crowd.
  • Blending: looks like normal armor, and detect magic doesn't reveal the property. At the command word it looks like ordinary clothes to everyone, while still working normally. Only true seeing shows what it really is.
  • Fear: looks like normal armor; detect magic shows only that it is magical. At the command word, the wearer gives off a fear aura in a 30-foot radius: every creature in it saves versus spell or flees in panic for one turn. The wearer is immune. Each use costs a charge. When the charges run out it is normal +1 armor, and it can't be recharged. The book prints two charge counts in the same paragraph: "2d4 fear charges when found" and "2d10 charges when found".
  • Possession: seems normal magic armor, with the plus from Table 76. But its maker put more than effort into it: the armor took in his personality and life force. The first time it is put on, and once a day after, the DM secretly rolls a save versus spell for the wearer. On a failure the life force begins to possess him. This is gradual, taking 3d4 days: first a few odd habits and possessiveness about the armor, then he drifts from old friends and haunts, wanders the streets looking for places the armorer knew, and has memories that aren't his. He refuses to take the armor off. At the end he is wholly possessed: he doesn't know his old friends or his own past, perhaps not even his class abilities, and may take a new name, a new alignment or a new class's abilities. If not freed, he becomes a non-player character under the DM's control. An exorcism spell breaks the possession and destroys the armor's personality. Dispel magic frees him long enough to take the armor off, but doesn't remove traits he has already absorbed. If the possessing influence is destroyed, the armor loses all its magic.
  • Healing: seems normal magic armor, but once a day, without warning and at no set time, it heals the wearer 2d6 points, wanted or not. Each healing uses a charge; it has 3d10 charges when found. When they run out it is +1 armor.

Weapons of quality

These aren't magical, just exceptionally well made. A character with the weaponsmith or bowyer proficiency can make them (see the proficiency).

  • Swords and miscellaneous melee weapons: forged of the finest steel, honed razor sharp, of the finest woods and so on. +1 to hit only. Worth 2d6 times the normal price.
  • Bows, crossbows and slings: perfectly balanced for pull and weight. Each range counts as the next shorter one for to-hit modifiers: short and medium both count as short, and long counts as medium. Beautifully made, worth 2d4 times the normal price.
  • Missile weapons: balanced to fly true and strike hard. +1 to hit only. Some are fancifully and tastefully decorated. Worth 2-5 times the normal price.
  • Martial arts weapons: made by martial arts masters who understand what the style demands. +1 to hit only, for someone trained in a martial arts style. Usually plain and simple looking; those who know martial arts will pay 2-5 times the normal price.
  • Ninja weapons: made with the ninja in mind. Ordinary looking, but razor sharp and finely balanced: +1 damage. Very light and compact; large ones come apart into small, easily hidden pieces and go back together in one round.

Magic properties

  • +1, +2, +3: the bonus applies to both to-hit and damage.
  • +1, +2, +3 damage: extra damage only, no bonus to hit.
  • +1, +2, +3 to hit: bonus to hit only, no extra damage.
  • +1, +2 vs. S: +1 to hit and damage against man-sized and larger creatures, +2 against smaller ones.
  • +1, +2 vs. L: +1 to hit and damage against man-sized and smaller creatures, +2 against larger ones.
  • -1, cursed: can't be told from a normal +1 weapon until used in earnest combat. A cursed bow is -1 to hit, and on a to-hit roll of 1 the missile comes back full force on the archer, for normal damage. A cursed melee weapon is -1 to hit; once picked up and used, the owner prefers it to all others and never willingly discards or ignores it. Remove curse frees him.
  • Accuracy +3: +3 to hit and damage, and every range counts as short (no range modifier).
  • Balance: seems a normal +1 weapon and is +1 to hit and damage. Carried, it gives exceptional balance: ninja get +10% to tightrope walking, and wherever balance matters (teetering on the edge of a pit and so on) the character automatically gets a save versus death to regain his footing, the weapon shifting or tugging him the fraction of an inch he needs. On a failed save he suffers the normal result.
  • Dancing: seems a +2 weapon and is +2 to hit and damage in hand. At the command word the martial arts weapon leaps to life and fights through the forms of the character's style, with as many attacks as his style gives and his chance to hit. He must have fought with it in the round before he speaks the word. It stays within five feet of him, fights for 2-5 rounds, then returns to his hands. The word works once a turn. It does nothing unless he knows a martial arts style that teaches this weapon.
  • Detection: +1 to hit and damage, and detects one kind of thing (roll 1d8: 1 evil, 10' radius; 2 good, 10' radius; 3 poison, by touch; 4 life forms, 10' radius; 5 back attacks, 1' range; 6 invisible creatures and objects, 10' radius; 7 traps, 5' radius; 8 secret doors, 10' radius). The character must hold it and speak the command word; if the answer is yes, the weapon tugs gently toward what it found.
  • Disruption: works exactly as the DMG's mace of disruption.
  • Distance +1: +1 to hit and damage, and every range category doubles.
  • Flame: +1 to hit and damage. At the command word it bursts into magic flame: +2d4 damage on a hit, sets combustibles alight 40% of the time, and sheds light in a 15-foot radius. It burns until the word is spoken again, and never harms the weapon, whatever it is made of.
  • Intelligence: +3 to hit and damage, with intelligence and powers as an intelligent sword, but never communicating beyond semi-empathy. Intelligence is 12-17 (1d6+11). Use the DMG's intelligent sword rules for its powers.
  • Silence: +1 to hit and damage. Held, it wraps the character in a muffling field that deadens (but doesn't stop) the sound he makes, while he still hears normally. A ninja gets +15% to move silently and +20% to hide in shadows. Sound-based attacks do half or no damage. The field covers only him and what he carries: something he drops or knocks over makes its normal noise. This property is explained in the book but isn't on Table 79.
  • Slaying: a +3 weapon marked or made in a distinctive way, easy to pick out from similar weapons. The markings show what kind of creature it slays. On a hit against that kind of creature, the creature dies at once, and the missile then loses all its magic. Possible creatures include bajang, bushi, dragons, elementals, giants, hengeyokai, hu hsien, humans, kalau, korobokuru, kuei, nats, ninja, ogre magi, ogres, oni, p'oh, samurai, shukenja, sohei, spiders, spirit folk, wu jen and yakuza; the DM can add to, change or limit the list to suit his campaign.
  • Speed: +1 to hit and damage. A speed bow (bow, crossbow or pellet bow) fires at double the normal rate and nocks or cocks itself, so the user automatically fires one shot first in the round. If surprised he can't react in time, though under complete surprise he can fire one shot in the second segment. A speed throwing weapon leaps from the hand: at the start of any round he holds it, he attacks first if he throws it. A speed martial arts weapon doubles the attacks his style allows with it, if he knows a style that teaches the weapon.
  • Unbreakable: counts as +2 to hit and damage. The weapon breaker special maneuver can't break it, and a foe who tries has a 75% chance of breaking his own weapon instead.
  • Venom: exactly like the DMG's dagger of venom.

Source: OA p.98-99 (Combat; Summary of the Combat Sequence; Surprise and Iaijutsu; Initiative Modifiers). Rewritten in plain words. Adapted for OA Lite.

OA uses the normal 1eFRPG rules for combat, with the additions below for these styles and techniques.

The combat round, with the OA additions

  1. Surprise: each side checks; characters are normally surprised on 1-2 on 1d6. Sometimes surprise isn't possible because of visibility, surroundings, noise and so on. OA: iaijutsu can change the roll (below).
  2. Declare actions: players say what their characters will try. OA: they must also say if a character is trying to subdue, disarm or unhorse an opponent.
  3. Initiative: if no one is surprised, each side rolls 1d6; the higher roll goes first this round. OA: kensai and wu jen can modify the roll (below).
  4. The winning side acts: OA: first, any kensai or wu jen whose modified roll beats both sides acts. Then each character on the winning side rolls 1d20 to hit, compared to the target's armor class on his class's combat table; equal or higher, with strength, magic and other modifiers, is a hit. OA: some characters must say whether they are using ki power before rolling. Targets of spells make their saving throws. OA: a shukenja must say whether he is using ki power before any saving throw is made. Roll damage for each hit, adding strength, magic weapons, weapons of quality and ki powers, and subtract it from the target's hit points. OA: subdual damage isn't subtracted but noted separately.
  5. The losing side acts as in step 4.

Surprise and iaijutsu

A character with the iaijutsu proficiency draws his weapon with lightning speed, which can catch others by surprise, but only in special situations: when a peaceful encounter suddenly turns violent. Picture a player character and a non-player character kneeling side by side in heated negotiations, swords sheathed. Tension rises, and the non-player character suddenly draws and lunges. Surprise is rolled to see who is ready, and how fast each can draw is everything.

  • If one has iaijutsu and the other doesn't, the one without it has -1 on his surprise roll.
  • If both have it, both have -1.
  • There is no modifier when weapons are already drawn, or the opponent has reason to expect an attack. It applies only when a peaceful situation erupts into bloodshed, especially from an unexpected quarter.

Initiative modifiers

Each round, unless someone is surprised, 1d6 is rolled for initiative, normally unmodified. But some people live by their quickness, and have trained their speed until they are more likely to strike the first, crucial blow.

  • Each side still rolls once. A character with a modifier applies it to his side's roll for his own actions only, so a round may split into more than two phases of attacks.
  • Ties aren't rerolled: everyone tied acts at the same instant. Damage and spell effects against a character acting at the same moment don't take effect until he finishes his own action; then he suffers them normally.
  • If one side's roll beats even the highest modified roll on the other side, the whole winning side acts in any order it likes, all before the other side.

Example: a 1st level kensai, samurai and shukenja meet a band of hostile samurai. The player characters roll 3; the non-player characters roll 4. The kensai (modified to 4) and the non-player characters strike first, at the same instant, then the samurai and shukenja. Had the other band included a kensai, he would have struck first (on 5), then the rest of his band and the player character kensai together, then the surviving player characters.

pages.name: Horseback, Unhorsing, Disarming, Subduing and the Psychic Duel

text.content:
Source: OA p.99-101 (Missile Fire from Horseback; Unhorsing; Disarming; Subduing Opponents; The Psychic Duel; Table 67). Rewritten in plain words. Table 67 was checked against the page image. Adapted for OA Lite.

Shooting from horseback

The mounted archer is central to the armies of the steppes and plains. Hordes of riders on swift ponies sweep across the plains, shooting from the saddle; warriors practice until they can hit targets at full gallop with great bows. It is no show: horse archers gallop at the enemy, loose their arrows, wheel away out of reach of foot archers, and raid camps without stopping. When armies of heavy foot and knights marched against them, disaster was the usual result: their slogging ranks were thinned by arrows, the riders galloped off before the footmen could shoot back, and knights who charged were simply avoided and shot down.

  • Anyone can shoot from a horse that is standing still.
  • Shooting from a moving horse takes the horsemanship proficiency, since a bow needs both hands and the rider must guide the horse with his knees. The DM can rule that very rough ground (rocky slopes, thick brush and so on) needs the reins, which stops shooting.
  • Rate of fire from horseback is half normal: 2/1 becomes 1/1, 3/1 becomes 3/2, and so on.
  • The rider has a penalty to hit for the horse's speed (Table 67), added to the modifiers for range, weapon against armor type and so on.
  • In a round he shoots, the horse can only turn slightly, at most 30 degrees either way. Sharper turns or maneuvers stop him shooting.
  • The same rules apply on any horse-like creature that horsemanship covers.

Unhorsing

Where horsemen are so formidable, footmen want them off their horses, where they can be outnumbered and overpowered.

  • Killing the horse puts the rider on foot at once, by missile or melee. But horses are valuable, and often the prize the attackers want, so this is a last resort.
  • Struck by a rider: when a rider is hit by a melee weapon 3 feet or longer, wielded by another mounted character, on a natural 20, he may fall. Without horsemanship he falls, taking an extra 1d3 damage. With it, he rolls against the proficiency: success keeps him in the saddle (he still takes the hit's damage); failure means he falls as above.
  • Struck by a footman: a footman with a melee weapon 5 to 9 feet long has the same chance as a rider. One with a weapon 10 feet or longer unhorses on 16-20 on 1d20 (25%). Either way the rider gets his horsemanship roll to stay on.
  • Diving from the saddle: a rider can pull alongside another and leap at him. A hit means he has grabbed him; a miss means he falls to the ground. The grabbed rider rolls against horsemanship: on a failure both fall, taking 1d6 each; on a success he stays in the saddle with the attacker hanging off his side. The attacker must hit again every turn to force another proficiency roll; if he misses, he falls (and takes damage). Meanwhile the rider can strike at him at -2 to hit.
  • Pulled down by footmen: only man-sized or larger creatures can try; larger ones count as two men. The footman must grab the rider as he passes with a to-hit roll at -2 if the horse moves 6" or less, -4 at 7" to 12", or -6 faster than 12". If he hits, the rider rolls against horsemanship to stay on. If the attempt fails and the horse is moving faster than 12", the horse gets a free set of attacks on the footman. Each extra footman grabbing (up to 4) gives -1 to the rider's roll. A rider pulled down by more than one man takes no damage, since he likely lands on someone. Eight men around a horse can pull down horse and rider together. Horse and rider attack normally throughout.
  • Prepared defenses: given time and materials, ropes strung between trees at rider height, tripwires and similar tricks can unhorse riders; the DM decides how well they work. Sharpened stakes stop charges: two men can stake a 10-foot square in an hour with stakes 4 to 5 feet long, if bamboo or light wood is at hand. Stakes are easy to see and avoid by turning aside, or a rider can urge his horse through, which takes a proficiency roll as for a jump or leap. A horse that enters the stakes hits 1d4-1 (0-3) stakes per 10 feet of depth, one fewer with chain barding and two fewer with plate, each doing 2d6 damage to the horse.
  • These rules work for any ridden creature.

Disarming

Sometimes characters need to disarm a foe: a charmed friend attacking them, or someone they want to capture without getting badly hurt.

  • With a weapon: the character needs a melee weapon at least as big as the victim's, and must say at the start of the round that he is disarming. He rolls to hit normally but does no damage; instead the victim saves versus petrification or drops the weapon, which lands 1d6 feet away. Picking it up takes a round.
  • Bare-handed: use the weaponless combat rules in the UA, or martial arts if the character has it. With martial arts he can knock loose a weapon of any size, the same way as with a weapon, but the victim gets +2 on his save.
  • Two-handed weapons: a success knocks loose only one hand, so two successes in the same round are needed. With only one, the foe simply regrips at the end of the round.

Subduing

Sometimes the goal is to beat an opponent without killing him: shukenja are normally forbidden to kill, and prisoners and hostages are only useful alive.

  • Only creatures of at least low intelligence can be subdued. Those of genius intelligence or higher are subdued only if they choose to surrender; they know what happens to most prisoners. Any creature or non-player character can be subdued, but a player character can never be forced to submit; surrendering is the player's choice.
  • Subduing must be declared at the start of the fight. Attackers then strike with the back, flat, haft, butt, pommel or hilt. Roll damage normally: 1/4 is lost from hit points, and 3/4 is subdual damage, recorded separately.
  • When subdual damage passes the creature's full (not current) hit points, it is subdued and surrenders. If anyone attacks it for normal damage after subduing was declared, it won't surrender: all subdual damage vanishes and it is fought normally.
  • A subdued creature stops fighting and drops its weapons. If the characters can talk with it, they can demand an oath: a task or promise such as "Leave this province never to return", "Go to your lord and tell him of your humiliating defeat", or "Swear never to haunt this place again". The DM secretly makes it save versus death. If it fails the save, it obeys. (OA rolls against honor for creatures that have it; OA Lite has no honor, so every creature saves.) Otherwise it pretends to agree and plans revenge.
  • Instead, the victor can keep it captive. It escapes at the first chance, staying meek only while its captors keep the upper hand.

The psychic duel

Two fierce samurai face off in a dusty street. Neither moves; only flies buzz; sweat runs down their mustaches. Then one bobs his head in a bow, turns, and slips away into the crowd. The other grins: he has won without touching his sword.

That is a psychic duel: a hidden struggle of will, courage, skill and determination between proud warriors. Any race or class can try it; it isn't psionic. It shows in a faint grimace, a flicker of an eyelid, a twitching muscle. Will he attack with wild abandon? Is he calm and sure of his skill? Will he risk certain death? A character who shows such qualities may win without a fight, and the wise man knows when he is outmatched and yields before it comes to blows.

  • When: only between intelligent humans or humanoids, one against one. Never between friends or companions. Not if they have already crossed weapons in this encounter, and not if others attack them during it. So not in the heat of battle, but perhaps as a challenge before it, or to put a swaggering bully in his place.
  • How: both spend the round within 10 feet of each other, focusing their will, then each saves versus death. Kensai get +2 against non-kensai. One success and one failure: the one who succeeded wins. Both fail: no one wins. Both succeed: they stay locked together for another round. Anyone who breaks off and attacks before it is settled loses; his nerve broke.
  • Winning: the winner has faced down his foe. (OA awards honor for winning, which OA Lite leaves out.)
  • Losing: the loser either retreats or attacks anyway. If he attacks, he is -1 on initiative, to-hit and saving throw rolls for the whole fight. There is no surprise roll, since both are ready.

Source: OA p.101-102 and 105-106 (Martial Arts; Styles; Stunning and Incapacitating; Learning Martial Arts; Multiple Styles and Combining Styles; Table 68). Rewritten in plain words. Table 68 was checked against the page image. Adapted for OA Lite.

In the martial arts the body itself becomes a weapon that can beat foes who seem better armed and armored: hands, feet, legs, arms, head, any part. It takes rigorous training and great physical and mental discipline to master the styles, maneuvers and feats: to anticipate, harden the body, shut out pain, and call up energy from deep within. It demands real commitment.

Where they come from:

  • Philosophy: people in the lands where they arose believe in the forces of nature, not as ideas but as energies charging everything around them. A person is part of those forces and can draw on them, and strives to live in harmony with them, through offerings, prayers or understanding. First he must master and harmonize the forces within himself. Tools change nature but stand outside that harmony, so knowing one's own body leads to fighting without weapons.
  • Religion: several faiths teach that the world is passing and possessions have no lasting worth, only a person's inner qualities. Relying on a weapon is relying on the material world, so devout followers develop their own abilities instead.
  • Law: where they arose, lords often pass harsh edicts against owning weapons, especially in conquered or troublesome provinces, with punishments up to torture and execution. Commoners found other ways to defend themselves.

In time these skills became widespread and honorable. Styles and training were made regular, studied scientifically and religiously, until unarmed fighting became an art that, practiced rightly, leads the student toward self-perfection. Every land developed its own styles, to counter local weapons and copy local beasts, and every master developed his own moves, so two masters of one style may fight quite differently. Arguments over which style was best were common, and challenges between schools drew hundreds of onlookers.

At root, martial arts teach a fighter to avoid being hurt. Some styles do this defensively, turning aside or dodging; some aggressively, holding that attack is the best defense; some by mastering many weapons. Techniques include punches, blocks, kicks, pushes, throws, holds, locks and dodges. "Unarmed" is a misnomer: students often learn common and unusual weapons, which take the same discipline as the open-hand forms and are taught only as part of a style. A peasant handed a tui-fa is no threat; a master with one is deadly.

These rules don't list every move of a style. A style is defined by its effects in play: attacks, damage, armor class and principal attack form. As characters rise in level they may learn the special maneuvers of their style, but only with dedication and training.

Styles

A style has five features: number of attacks, damage, armor class, principal attack form and special maneuvers. Every combination is a different style, learned separately. Styles often have descriptive or poetic names: animals (Snake, Monkey, Tiger), poetry (Eight Drunken Fairies), or descriptions (Empty Hand, Springing Legs, Eight Fists). Some are highly defensive and rely on inner power; others are aggressive, with hard, sudden attacks.

  • Number of attacks works as in normal combat, but depends on the style, so a character may attack more, fewer or the same number of times as with weapons. It applies only when fighting in that style.
  • Damage is the die rolled on a hit. Defensive styles usually do little; offensive ones more.
  • Armor class is the protection the training gives, by avoiding, turning or withstanding blows.
  • Principal attack form is the body part the style uses most. As long as it is free, the character can attack effectively: a karate fighter, who uses his fists, can still attack with his legs held.
  • Special maneuvers are the secrets of the art: fantastic feats such as backward kick, sticking touch, great throw and ironskin, hard to learn (see Creating a Style).

Some styles list maneuvers above difficulty 1 without the easier ones of that method (Kung-fu's Kick 2, for example); the progression rule counts across all methods, so these are as printed. Each style is also an item in the OA Lite Martial Arts compendium.

Stunning and incapacitating

Every style can stun or incapacitate a man-sized foe. On an unmodified 20 to hit, the victim saves versus paralyzation. If he saves, he just takes normal damage. If he fails, compare the number rolled on his save to his hit dice or level: if it is lower, he is stunned for 1d6 rounds; if higher, he is out for 1-3 hours. Creatures with +4 or more on their hit dice count as one die higher.

Example: a martial artist rolls 20 against a lizard man, which fails its save with a 2. That equals the lizard man's 2+1 hit dice, so it is stunned for 1d6 rounds. Had it rolled 6, it would have been out for 1-3 hours. (The book doesn't say what happens when the roll exactly equals the hit dice except through this example, which treats it as stunned.)

Learning martial arts

A martial arts style costs a proficiency slot like any other proficiency, but it is harder to learn and has extra requirements.

Finding a master. "Master" is an honorary title, not a class, and says nothing of skill or level. A master might be a peasant, a hermit developing his own style, a traveling bushi, a teacher with a school in a town, a famous samurai, or a temple priest teaching his followers. Some masters are brilliant and famous, some skilled, some barely able to teach the basics, and some incompetent behind an impressive title; students find out as they study.

  • Masters can be hard to find. Many guard their art as a secret for a chosen few (many styles have died with their masters), don't display their skill because it would be proud and boastful (and might anger the gods), or hope never to have to use it. Some believe their art can be learned only in tranquil seclusion deep in the mountains.
  • Politics hides them too: conquered peoples may be forbidden their arts, and nervous emperors, warlords or daimyos may destroy powerful temples, the usual centers of training, scattering masters and students into secret societies.
  • Still, towns and cities may have schools run by well-known masters that students travel far to reach. Characters will hear of such schools, and sometimes of the secretive masters.

Being accepted.

  • A character with no martial arts presents himself humbly and respectfully, with a 10% chance of being accepted at once. Usually he is politely sent away. He then courts the master, returning with small gifts; each visit that pleases the master (and stays respectful) adds 10% to the chance. He can keep returning until accepted, or until he offends the master, who will then never take him.
  • A character who already knows some martial arts can challenge the master, which is always accepted. The master decides whether he or a student fights; if the challenger isn't well known, a student is assigned, which is customary and no insult. Challenges are fought to subdue (usually preferred, sparing needless killing) or to the death; a death in a challenge isn't a crime and the victor is rarely punished. Crowds may gather to watch. If the challenger wins, the master accepts him (and may hope to learn from him). If he loses, he can leave and return when more skilled, or humbly beg to be accepted, which works especially well after a humiliating defeat.

What the master knows. The master always knows the basics (armor class, attacks, damage). For weapons, the DM counts the style's weapons and rolls the smallest die equal to or above that number: the result is how many he knows. He does the same for the style's special maneuvers. The master knows maneuvers from the easiest up, under the same rule as students, and never learns more unless the DM rules otherwise.

Training.

  • After at least a month with the master, the character spends one slot and gains the basics: armor class, number of attacks and damage, but no special maneuvers or weapons.
  • He is then free to travel and adventure, but must practice at least an hour a day and spend six hours a week with his master; otherwise he can't add maneuvers or weapons.
  • Each further slot adds one special maneuver or weapon of the style. He doesn't suddenly know it; he is assumed to have been practicing. No more than two slots can be spent on one style per level.
  • Maneuvers must be learned in order of difficulty: all difficulty 1 maneuvers before any difficulty 2, and so on.
  • Once he has learned all the master knows, he can seek another master who knows more, or teaches another style.

More than one style

  • A character can learn several styles, with a master for each, enough slots and enough dedication.
  • In a fight he chooses one style and has only its abilities and maneuvers, except maneuvers that are always in effect. He can change style from round to round.
  • Once he has two or more styles and has learned all their masters know, he can create his own style, mixing their elements as he likes (one style's armor class with another's attacks and damage, say) and combining all the maneuvers he knows. He can teach it as a master.

Source: OA p.102-103 (Creating a Style; Notes Regarding Style Combination Table; Special Maneuvers; Tables 69 and 70). Rewritten in plain words. Tables 69 and 70 were checked against the page images. Adapted for OA Lite.

The DM is encouraged to create new styles for his campaign, taught by non-player character masters. You never know when a hermit in the hills has developed a new fighting style.

1. Form: hard, soft or both

  • Hard styles use muscle and bone for power, with direct movements, and are generally offensive.
  • Soft styles draw on inner power (though they still condition the muscles), with fluid, circular movements, and are generally defensive: they turn the attacker's force against him and strike only once he has committed himself. Training is more mental, teaching the student to focus his inner power.
  • Hard/soft styles combine both: gentle circular defense with swift direct attacks, physical training balanced with mental.
  • Any style can use a number of unusual weapons.

2. Principal method

The principal method is how the style most often attacks: kicking styles kick a lot, throwing styles rely on grappling and leverage, and so on. Every style also uses moves from other methods, since relying on one would mean certain defeat.

3. Work out the style

  • Pick one form and one principal method.
  • Armor class: add the two AC mods and subtract the total from 10.
  • Attacks: add the two attacks mods; that is the attacks per round in this style only, not in any other style or with normal weapons.
  • Damage: add the two damage mods and round up to the nearest die used in the game: 4 is 1d4, 5 or 6 is 1d6.
  • Body part: the method's body part. As long as it is free, the character can attack effectively in the style. (Throwing uses the whole body.)
  • Weapons: roll 1d4 and subtract 2 for how many weapons the style teaches, chosen from the weapons usable only with martial arts.

4. Special maneuvers

Special maneuvers take intensive study but give better-than-normal results. Some are actions tried during a fight (flying kick, one finger); some, once learned, are always in effect (ironskin, blind fighting).

  • A combat maneuver costs one or more of the character's attacks that round, and is risky: failure often leaves him exposed.
  • A movement maneuver counts as movement, so he makes no attacks that round unless the maneuver says otherwise.
  • Maneuvers are grouped by principal method and marked hard, soft or hard/soft, matching the style's form. Soft styles mostly use soft maneuvers and hard styles hard ones, but they can cross over.
  • Mental and Physical Training maneuvers can be learned in any style, through its practice and discipline.

Choosing the style's maneuvers:

  • Roll 1d8: that many maneuvers come from the style's principal method or from Mental and Physical Training.
  • Then roll 1-3 more from other methods (or Mental and Physical Training again). Most styles borrow a few to round out their tactics.
  • The number by each maneuver is its difficulty; lower is easier. The style's maneuvers must run upward from 1, but the run can cross methods and include several of the same difficulty. For example: circle kick (1), flying kick (2), all-around sight (2), backward kick (3). A character learns them in that order; he can learn a harder one only once the easier ones are learned.
  • Maneuvers aren't gained when the style is first learned; see Learning Martial Arts on the Martial Arts page.

OA Lite adds the OA races, classes, proficiencies, martial arts, spells, weapons, armor and equipment, magic items and monsters to the 1e FRPG system, for use in any campaign. It leaves out the Eastern Lands setting, the family, honor and society rules, OA's own money and the running-the-game chapters (events and encounters). Everything is restated in plain words with the book's numbers. You need the book for its original text.

Turning it on

  • Switch the module on in Manage Modules, then accept the offer to build the OA Lite compendia. They can be rebuilt at any time from Configure Settings, 1e FRPG: OA Lite, Rebuild OA Lite compendia (this replaces the copies in the world).
  • Don't run OA Lite and the full OA module together: they add the same races and classes. If both are on, OA Lite stays off and says so.
  • The world setting OA races and classes only is off by default, so the OA races and classes sit alongside the PHB and UA ones. Turn it on to leave only the OA ones in the lists.

On the character sheet

  • Races: human, korobokuru, hengeyokai and the three spirit folk, with the OA class limits and ability ranges.
  • Classes: barbarian, bushi, kensai, monk, ninja, samurai, shukenja, sohei, wu jen and yakuza, with their experience tables, hit dice, attacks, saving throws and spell tables. Kensai and monk armor class, bushi armor class improvement, monk movement, barbarian constitution hit points, wu jen +1 hit point per die, ninja split-class hit points and the ninja backstab multiplier are applied automatically.
  • OA tab: the class abilities for the current level, the proficiency pool, martial arts style and maneuvers, hengeyokai animal form, wu jen spells known and taboos, and yakuza contacts.
  • Proficiencies from the OA Lite Proficiencies compendium use their base number: roll that or more on 1d20, +1 per later slot, never needing less than 3.
  • Martial arts: drag a style from the OA Lite Martial Arts compendium to the Weapons list to attack with it.

What changes from the full OA module

  • No honor, family or birth: there is no honor score, birth rank, ancestry or birthright, and no Roll birth button. Class rules that worked through honor say so where they come up; the DM judges those cases (for example, when a samurai becomes a ronin).
  • Prices in standard coins: every price is converted from OA's coins with the real values in OA Table 46: 1 fen = 1 cp, 1 yuan = 5 cp, 1 tael = 10 sp, 1 ch'ien = 5 gp. Each price is given in the largest coin that divides it evenly.
  • Treasure: use the DMG treasure types, including for the treasure letters of the OA monsters. Table 86 (OA magic items) is kept as a roll table.
  • Languages: OA's own trade and court languages are left out; use the campaign's common tongue in their place.

Things done by hand

  • Armor pieces (OA Table 53): the sheet counts only the best single armor item, so enter the combined armor class of the pieces as an armor class override or a miscellaneous adjustment.
  • Weights: the book prints weights for weapons (Table 49), armor (Table 54) and barding. Everything else is marked "unspecified", meaning no weight is printed; enter one if your table wants it. Animals, vehicles and services don't count toward load.
  • Sohei spells: the system has no sohei mark, so each spell sohei can use says so at the top of its description.
  • Wu jen elements are noted at the top of each wu jen spell.
  • Two-handed weapons: the book marks them in bold on Table 49, but the scan doesn't show which reliably, so they aren't marked (see Weapons).

Where the book disagrees with itself

Every number was checked against the page images. Where the text and a table disagree, the table is used and both are noted on the page, marked "as printed": for example the XP bonus abilities (text against Table 12), the kensai armor class steps (Table 19), and the calligraphy base number (Table 61 says 18, an example says 17).
